items.body:
Aldi is recruiting for 600 new roles at its new automated Distribution Centre in Bardon, Leicestershire, as the supermarket continues to build its operations at the site over the next year.
The Bardon Distribution Centre began operations in May 2026 and is Aldi’s first automated distribution centre in the UK. The UK’s biggest discount grocer has invested more than £500m into the site, as part of its £1.6bn UK expansion plan. In September, the retailer reached another milestone in the ramp up with the start of fresh produce operations at the site. Once fully operational, Bardon will be the biggest supermarket distribution centre in the country, capable of moving around seven million pallets each year, supporting stores across the Midlands and beyond.
The opportunities on offer, with start dates over the next year, span warehouse operations, logistics and transport, offering successful applicants the chance to join the Aldi team and develop skills in modern warehouse technology.
The roles currently being recruited include:
- Warehouse Pickers
- Warehouse Operations Assistants
- Transport Assistants
Successful applicants will benefit from competitive rates of pay. Warehouse Operations Assistants currently earn from £13.31 to £16.64 per hour, depending on shift pattern, with competitive salaries also available across transport and other operational roles.
Jonathan Heaton, managing director of Bardon at Aldi, said: “We’re really looking forward to welcoming more people to the Bardon team as recruitment continues over the coming months. It’s a fantastic opportunity for anyone looking to build a career in logistics, whether they’re just starting out or bringing previous experience, and to build the technical skills that are increasingly valuable in modern supply chain operations.
“We’re also proud to be working with local colleges and employment partners to help create opportunities for people across Leicestershire. Every new colleague joining Bardon will play an important role in supporting Aldi’s continued growth and helping us build our future distribution network.”
Minister for Employment, Andrew Western MP, said: “This is great news for people across Leicestershire.
“We are determined to get people back to work in every postcode by transforming Jobcentre Plus and accelerating our £2.5 billion youth employment support package, creating up to one million opportunities for young people to earn or learn.”
Aldi is one of 40 retailers that recently signed up to ‘Opening Shift’, a partnership with Government and the BRC to offer 11,000 work experience placements for 18-24 year olds. The scheme’s target is to create 100,000 jobs for young people in the sector by the end of this Parliament.
Those interested in applying for a role at Bardon can visit: Careers Vacancies in Bardon – Aldi Recruitment GB

items.body:
Analysis of the UK beauty market by ecommerce optimisation specialists MediaVision found that Boots has emerged as the clear leader in the UK beauty market, as new findings reveal a significant gap between the high-street retailer and its closest competitors.
The figures, which measure the proportion of searches attracted by leading beauty brands and retailers, show that Boots accounts for 32% share of brand search, significantly ahead of Superdrug at 12%. The gap widens further across the rest of the market, with Sephora ranking third at 3%, followed by Lookfantastic, Space NK, and Charlotte Tilbury, respectively.
Together, the rankings point to a highly concentrated beauty landscape, with Boots and Superdrug attracting significantly more consumer attention than the retailers that follow.
Boots lead extends well beyond high-street
Boots’ position is particularly notable in an increasingly fragmented beauty market, where brands are competing for consumer attention across search, social media, entertainment and retail. Despite this growing competition, the findings suggest large multi-category retailers continue to command significant levels of consumer demand, with Boots maintaining a considerable lead.
The retailer has also expanded its presence beyond the traditional high-street, positioning itself at the center of beauty culture through entertainment partnerships, creator content, and consumer-facing campaigns. From its Love Island partnership and creator-led ‘shop with me’ content to campaigns such as ‘Dan Won’t Burn’, Boots has continued to find new ways to engage shoppers across different channels.
Katie Gloyne, SEO Manager at MediaVision, comments: “The retail landscape is increasingly competitive. The brands maintaining the biggest share of search are those that build sustained consumer awareness through distinctive retail experiences, product innovation, and credible partnerships with search data to anticipate demand and sustain consumer visibility across multiple channels. In beauty, the strongest performers are not just capturing demand; they are leading the conversations.”
Convenience and choice continue to drive beauty shoppers
With more brands and products to choose from than ever, beauty shoppers are increasingly option-rich but time-poor, making convenience an important part of the shopping experience. The dominance of Boots and Superdrug suggests consumers continue to value retailers that make it easier to browse different brands, categories, and price points in one place.
For Boots, this is reflected in an evolving beauty offering of more than 500 brands, giving shoppers access to both affordable and premium products in one place. Its Advantage Card data also provides insight into changing customer interests, allowing the retailer to deliver more relevant and personalised promotions alongside its extensive product range.
Superdrug’s position as Boots’ closest competitor reinforces the continued appeal of this model. The retailer similarly combines established beauty brands with affordable own-brand ranges across skincare, cosmetics and haircare, while initiatives such as Superdrug Presents bring brands, product discovery, masterclasses and beauty experiences together beyond the shop floor.
Together, their performance suggests that value, convenience, and breadth of choice remain important to UK beauty shoppers, even as the wider market becomes increasingly crowded with specialist and emerging brands.
Louis Venter, founder & CEO at MediaVision, comments: “The UK beauty sector is evolving rapidly, and the brands that understand where consumer demand is moving are best positioned to capture future growth.
“Established awareness remains an advantage, but the brands responding fastest to changing consumer interests will increasingly be the ones winning attention.”

items.body:
The Retail Trust has teamed up with SAI, the leading active intelligence solution for stores, which has become an official partner of the charity as part of SAI’s work to support retail workers’ safety and wellbeing.
The move underscores SAI’s ongoing commitment to creating safer store environments for colleagues and customers through innovation, education and cultural change.
Already working with major grocers, including the Big Four, Iceland and Our Coop, as well as leading fashion brands, SAI’s solution unifies Loss Prevention (LP) and insight-led store operations. Using its patented Visual Language Model (VLM), the SAI One platform blends computer vision with GenAI to turn traditionally ‘passive’ store surveillance systems into an active, operational platform for real-time store intelligence.
As part of its work with leading brands on LP, SAI helps retailers reduce in-store violence, colleague abuse and shrink via its facial recognition technology (FRT) solution.  Born out of its founding principle that stores should be safe, community spaces free from crime and violence, SAI redistributes earnings from its violence prevention and FRT systems, setting them aside as a charitable trust.
It then uses these funds to support causes and charities that champion store safety, spanning colleague protection and wellbeing, rehabilitation projects supporting those with addictions who turn to shoplifting, and wider work with the policing and justice communities.
“When we launched SAI, we knew we never wanted to profit from violence – we’d rather there was no need for this technology at all,” Helen Wilde, Co-Founder & Chief Commercial Officer at SAI, explained.  “But with more and more retailers coming to us and needing our solution to tackle the problem, we decided to ensure revenues generated from this part of the business were used to do good and give back.”
In addition to supporting the charity, SAI will develop new ways to use intelligence help tackle repeat offenders.  With the top 10% of repeat retail offenders estimated to be responsible for between 68 – 70% of total in-store retail crime, its efforts will help reduce retail loss while making stores safer spaces for colleagues and communities.
Chris Brook-Carter, Chief Executive of the Retail Trust, said: “We are grateful for SAI’s support as we explore new ways of protecting retail workers against abuse, violence and theft and the impact this can have on their wellbeing.  Our partnership will build on the help the Retail Trust is already providing to hundreds of retailers and people working across the industry to create happier and safer retail workplaces.”
“We’ve long admired the work the Retail Trust does – both through the practical support it delivers to retail workers and by championing colleague wellbeing through awareness campaigns,” Helen added.  “This made partnering with them a natural step as we further our commitment to creating safer retail environments that support colleagues, customers and communities.”
The partnership with the Retail Trust comes as SAI prepares to launch its new Safer Stores initiative, which brings together diverse stakeholders – from major retailers to crime and justice bodies, rehabilitation groups and technology providers – in a shared mission to improve the safety of bricks-and-mortar environments.   Meanwhile, hundreds of businesses will back the Retail Trust’s Let’s Respect Retail campaign this Christmas by increasing employee support and calling for more respect from shoppers.

E-commerce and creative marketing agencies Say Yes and Verse have merged to create COMMON®, a design and build practice centred around commerce systems and digital experience, with migrating key accounts including Mitchells & Butlers, Myomaster and Union Coffee.
Co-founder and CEO, Phil Clark (Say Yes, Brave the Skies) has appointed seasoned Commerce specialist John Brolly (Geoffy, Athos Commerce, GPMD, Astound) into a newly created role of Chief Orchestration Officer to strengthen the existing senior team.
Tasked with seamlessly blending people and technology across the company, Brolly brings extensive experience from previous agency work across accounts including Percival, Montirex, Nicole Farhi, Puma, Size? and more.
Brolly said: “Bringing together expertise and talent from both agencies, COMMON will offer clients a single partner who holds the complete digital picture for commerce and experience from strategy through to orchestrated delivery, with the ability to scale at pace.”
He will work closely alongside Creative Lead Jordan Donnelly (Say Yes, Northern Artillery, Show + Tell, Creode, Awwwards Design Jury), who has previously worked on accounts including Viviene Westwood, Virgin Media and Sipsmith Gin, whilst Hayley Gardener takes up the role of Account Director at Common after almost a 10 year tenure at Verse leading the Mitchells & Butlers account.
Clark added: “Bringing together these two dynamic companies into one entity gives COMMON an edge, to offer clients a multitude of services and solutions, under one roof with craft at the core. We are people-first, bringing talent, creativity and experience to our clients, whilst utilising tech and systems for efficiency.”
The COMMON team is based across offices in London and York, backed by a team of 30 staff.
The COMMON team is also supported by peers across the superassembly® group including owner, co-founder, angel investor and technology advisor Sean Connell, and Group Communications & PR Director Emma Peel (UFC, IMG).

items.title: Retailers and union warn government not to raise business rates on shops
items.summary: Some of the UK’s largest retailers and Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, have warned the government not to raise business rates on shops as new research reveals that existing pressures could cost the sector around 90,000 jobs by 2031. The Retail Jobs Alliance, which includes Asda,… This story continues at Retailers and union warn government not to raise business rates on shops Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The Retail Jobs Alliance, which includes Asda, Kingfisher, Morrisons, Marks & Spencer, Primark, Sainsbury’s, Tesco, have today called on the government to exempt every bricks-and-mortar shop from the higher business rates multiplier introduced at last year’s Autumn Budget, ahead of the Budget on 28 October.
One in three retail workers are employed in the roughly 4,000 stores above the £500,000 rateable-value threshold.
New research from the Retail Jobs Alliance (RJA) predicts that, even with no further changes, existing cost pressures could cost the sector around 90,000 jobs by 2031, hitting young people and already-struggling towns hardest.
The figure projects forward the fall in retail employees in official HMRC and ONS data since 2023. The RJA warns that any further rise in the higher multiplier would push losses well beyond that.
The call follows Labour Party Conference, where delegates passed a motion tabled by Usdaw urging the government to exempt all bricks-and-mortar shops from the higher business-rates multiplier, something they have reiterated today.
On Tuesday, the chancellor met retail chief executives for pre-budget talks.
Martin Beck, chief economist at WPI Strategy, the consultancy which produced the analysis for the Retail Jobs Alliance, said: “Retailers are already absorbing additional costs and further increases in business rates would inevitably affect their ability to protect jobs, invest in stores and keep prices down.
“This new research highlights that ministers must proceed carefully, because when the cost of running shops rises, the consequences are felt not only by retail workers and high streets, but also by households through added pressure on the cost of living.”
Joanne Thomas, Usdaw general secretary said: “Job security is a key priority for our members. We support the government’s commitment to ‘growth in every postcode’ and the retail sector has a significant role to play in delivering this.
“We welcome the action the government has already taken in reducing business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues. Alongside this, Labour has a manifesto commitment to level the playing field between in-store retail and online giants.
“So, confirmation from the chancellor that the government will be producing a high streets strategy is welcome, but it is essential that it is linked to the wider industrial strategy, including exempting large retail premises from the higher rates multiplier.”
Kim Johnson, Labour MP for Liverpool Riverside, said: “This government’s manifesto promised to level the playing field between the high street and online giants, and that promise matters more than ever.
“Cutting business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues was absolutely right, but retail can’t be left picking up the bill for it. The sector already pays more than its fair share in business rates, risking jobs here in Liverpool Riverside and across the country.
“Retail is one of the first jobs many people ever have, and at a time of a NEETs crisis, we cannot afford for those pathways to be at risk.”
Retail already pays a share of business rates more than four times its contribution to UK GDP. The previous Autumn Budget alone added around £7bn in new costs and taxes to the sector, and the RJA warns that a further rise in the higher multiplier would leave large stores less able to protect jobs, hold down prices and invest in their communities.
The RJA warns that easing the burden on hospitality while raising it on retail risks weakening the very town centres the government wants to support. Large stores often act as anchors, drawing the footfall that sustains surrounding businesses and providing accessible employment opportunities.
The RJA and Usdaw have previously written to the government, urging ministers to exempt shops from the higher multiplier.

Customers shopping on M&S.com and through our app can now spread the cost in three interest free payments with Klarna, offering more flexibility in how they pay for the things they love.”

items.body:
Pricer selected by Orange for electronic shelf labels roll-out across store network in France
Pricer has been selected by Orange, a telecommunications operator in France, to digitalise its retail store network. The project encompasses 561 stores with an average size of 120 m² over the next two years.
The agreement covers the complete deployment of Pricer’s electronic shelf label (ESL) solution, including hardware, infrastructure, attachment solutions, installation, and cloud management via the Plaza platform under a long-term maintenance contract. It includes annual recurring SaaS and maintenance revenue. Orange chose Pricer following pilot programmes across multiple store locations.
“Orange is accelerating the transformation of its distribution network. Technological innovation is a central pillar of Orange’s distribution strategy. With this in mind, the deployment of electronic labels represents a major step forward, intended to improve customer experience in the stores and strengthen our advisors' operational efficiency. The Pricer solution offers multiple benefits: better visibility of offers, increased responsiveness to pricing and commercial changes, as well as reliable and up-to-date product information,” says Fabrice Barnéoud, Direction Commercial Grand Public at Orange.
“During the pilot phase conducted in our stores, Pricer emerged as the ideal partner. Beyond the technological quality of its solution, they demonstrated a strong operational commitment, with responsive and involved teams alongside our employees to ensure seamless integration and quality support. Thanks to this technology, and the dynamic and real-time promotion of our offers and products, Orange contributes to a truly optimal customer and advisor experience.”
“We are very proud to partner with Orange to digitalise their retail footprint across France,” says Vincent Raulin, Sales Director France, at Pricer. “This roll-out underlines the value of our solution beyond traditional retail environments. With a competitive and high performing offer, we are helping store teams work smarter and deliver better customer experiences.”
Roll-out is scheduled to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026, with the first 100 stores targeted for completion within the year. The project is due to wrap in 2028.

items.title: ‘I introduce myself to anyone who looks a bit jumpy’: a security guard’s take on anti-shoplifting fixes
items.summary: A professional reveals the most effective tricks of the trade, from a little bit of empathy to hi-tech cameras I’ve run into volatile thieves for years – from opportunistic phone snatchers to people ripping computers off desks and biofuel bandits trying to steal vats of used cooking oil – and every time I file an incident report, I try to make a recommendation for preventive measures. It’s safer to try to avoid a situation where things get physical with a suspected criminal. I don’t want to let my employers down, but I also don’t want anyone to have to go to hospital – myself included. Continue reading...
items.body:
I’ve run into volatile thieves for years – from opportunistic phone snatchers to people ripping computers off desks and biofuel bandits trying to steal vats of used cooking oil – and every time I file an incident report, I try to make a recommendation for preventive measures.
It’s safer to try to avoid a situation where things get physical with a suspected criminal. I don’t want to let my employers down, but I also don’t want anyone to have to go to hospital – myself included.
Greggs seems to be following a similar train of thought: earlier this year the chain phased out self-service cabinets in areas where shoplifting is rife and has installed safe pod “robocops” with 120-decibel sirens in some stores.
But snatch thefts seem to be on the rise everywhere, from “steaming” (large groups overwhelming a store) in city centres to machinery being swiped from rural farm shops. The cost of this crime – in terms of lost merchandise and measures to tackle it – further erodes margins at a time when retailers are battling higher employment costs and increases to business rates.
Customers, ever squeezed by rising energy bills, are becoming doubly impatient: those who are not tempted by grabbable goods are rightly affronted by measures such as sliding shields that seem to imply that everyone is a criminal.
But is it possible to make a store thief proof and welcoming to law-abiding clientele?
Discreet high technology is a happy medium. PTZ cameras (pan/tilt/zoom, which can be adjusted to track and focus on a single suspect) are one of the most-effective choices. They’re more efficient than fixed-camera CCTV, less controversial than AI surveillance and a serious upgrade on the convex mirror mounted at the end of the aisle in your local corner shop.
PTZ camera manoeuvrability means high-quality facial images, a must-have when trying to build evidence. Freeze-frames can also be used to generate stills that some premises owners choose to turn into warning posters, or share on a chat group with other local businesses.
My advice here is to be wary of GDPR regulations and remember that an incorrect time signature can render recordings inadmissible.
As useful as movable cameras are, they still require a human operator. Hiring guards can feel like a tax on businesses – but one that goes unpaid at considerable risk.
Ask anyone who lives in a village whether they’d prefer a CCTV camera or a “bobby on the beat” and the answer would be probably unanimously the latter.
The sight of a uniformed officer can be a strong deterrent. However, it comes with an upper limit. For example: if a 3,000 sq metre supermarket can accommodate 40,000 goods and 4,000 daily customers, one guard will not be able to cover it all.
It is also hard to identify which customers might be preparing to swipe something, especially given the rise of “middle-class shoplifting”. As someone whose job pays just above minimum wage, this is an interesting phenomenon.
I get that inflation presses down on all of us, but people further up the pyramid than me should know it won’t be shareholders or bonus-receiving bosses taking the hit for goods being pinched: it will be prices. Higher costs will further imperil the most vulnerable people who walk on site, the ones who already cannot afford bread or baby formula.
My best approach in these cases is empathy. I try to introduce myself to anyone who hangs around but looks jumpy; explain that every tap of my bank card makes me sweat too.
I also try to build local knowledge of repeat offenders: insight that made the bobbies on the beat so valuable. I know it won’t work against content creators who film me for “lols” while I’m administering first aid, and who half of all young Brits apparently want to emulate. I honestly fear them more than I do getting punched, stabbed or spat on.
But doing your revision pays off, especially when encountering an unsettled local resident with a penchant for threatening people with kitchen utensils. As the resident in question strode towards the premises one morning, my shiftmate quickly asked me whether I knew his name and address (I did).
“Morning, Mr Beddlington,” said my colleague as the resident got level with us and before he could grab his first frying pan. “Everything OK at Thorn Court today? Anything we can help with?”
The resident did an about-face and left the site. Loss prevention done low-cost and painlessly.
Names and addresses have been changed
What the Bouncer Saw: Life on the Front Line of the Security Business by George Bass is published by Hachette. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply

items.body:
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Best Use of Automation in Retail finalists announced including EE and Snag
We’re pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Best Use of Automation in the Retail Sector category. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector.
Check out a rundown of our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
Click here to book your place at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony on Wednesday, 4th November.
Our 2026 Best Use of Automation in the Retail Sector finalists as follows:
commercetools and Trail Appliances
Trail Appliances’ growth had created a problem: the commerce platform that once supported the business was now holding it back.
Complex promotions were difficult to deliver, development was increasingly time-consuming and the business needed greater freedom to innovate. Rather than accept those constraints, Trail Appliances rebuilt its commerce foundation with commercetools. Its flexible, API first approach allowed Trail’s development team to integrate best-of-breed technologies including Algolia and Voucherify and build around its specific needs.
The results: site load time fell 57%, conversion more than doubled, average SEO ranking improved approximately 200%, and revenue delivered strong double digit growth.
EE Retail
STAT! (Store Tools and Tasks, also inspired by the Latin statim, meaning ‘immediately’) is transforming how EE Retail manages operational activity.
Previously, tasks were spread across legacy automations, standalone apps and reporting tools. STAT! brings everything into one operational platform, with RALPH, the Retail Action Log (Pretty Helpful!), providing a single view of required actions. Tasks are scheduled or automatically triggered by operational data, helping stores act quickly while giving leaders live visibility of progress and risk.
The result is a simpler, smarter operation, improving on-time task completion and freeing store teams to focus on what matters most: customers.
Flip and Liquid I.V.
Liquid I.V. transformed its phone service from seasonal shutdowns into a channel available around the clock with Flip’s conversational AI. Facing summer call volumes four to five times normal levels, the brand deployed an AI agent in approximately 2.5 weeks to resolve customer requests while preserving its distinctive voice.
Today, 45% of calls are automated end to end, call abandonment has fallen 65%, and average handle time has dropped 81%. Phone lines remain open through peak summer demand; agents focus on complex customer needs; and conversation insights help teams identify product feedback, inventory concerns, and customer sentiment to inform decisions.
Furniture Connect
Furniture Connect is automating the end-to-end path from a finished furniture product to an ecommerce listing across multiple channels. Instead of requiring teams to coordinate photography, image editing, product preparation, catalogue content and channel formatting as separate tasks, the platform brings them into a single agent driven workflow.
Products can be processed in batches across whole ranges, imagery and variations generated from existing assets and ecommerce content prepared without the traditional production cycle. The result is less repetitive work, fewer handoffs and a much faster route to sale. Barker and Stonehouse can now bring more than 100 products online in a single week, where the process previously took months, while GJ Styles has cut the time involved in creating, preparing and uploading imagery by around 90%.
Goddiva
Goddiva has built an AI powered automation ecosystem connecting customer experience, retail intelligence and fashion product development. Simple customer inputs can trigger personalised product recommendations, sizing guidance, virtual try-on, order tracking and return support.
Behind this, Goddiva’s Global Product Analysis interprets sales, returns, stock, size and style performance to generate actionable trading intelligence. These insights connect with an AI powered Design Studio spanning trend forecasting, design exploration, costing, competitor analysis, size ratio planning, technical specifications and grading.
The result is a connected automation cycle where customer behaviour and retail performance increasingly inform what Goddiva designs, buys, produces and presents next.
Lily AI
Before a product reaches a consumer, an AI system increasingly decides whether it gets discovered or recommended. Lily AI has spent six years making products understandable to these systems.
Launched in August 2026, Lily Max turns that intelligence into action: agents identify missing product information, enrich it in consumer language, test changes against controls and deploy what works across paid media and AI discovery. Used by leading retailers and brands including Marks & Spencer, Vuori, Hibbett Sports, Shiseido and Coach, Lily has run 1,000+ controlled tests. Lily Max makes products understandable to AI, and proves the commercial impact when they are.
Optimum Retailing
Most AI merchandising tools produce plans, not planograms. Head office teams still turn each plan into a layout for every fixture in every store, by hand. Optimum Retailing automates that step.
Realgram AI reads sales, inventory and store conditions and generates a store specific planogram for every fixture, giving the best positions to high margin, fast selling products. Image recognition then verifies each set-up as the photo is taken. Print, distribution and store issues are managed in the same platform. Retailers using Realgram AI have seen 5 to 15% higher in-store revenue and 15 to 25% fewer labour hours.
Public Group
Public Group, which operates public.gr, public.cy and publicbusiness.gr, replaced more than ten disconnected tools and spreadsheets with Content Dashboard, an in-house platform that runs product content as a production line.
The platform decides for itself how much content each product justifies, from its category, its price and the data available - then builds to that level, sourcing specifications and images from manufacturer sites from 871 manufacturer brands, filling and validating attributes, and writing descriptions. It runs unattended overnight and through weekends; editors review finished work each morning, and content produced once serves all three storefronts.
Weekly backlogs of products waiting for content have fallen by around 80%, specification fill rates have moved from 40% to complete, and output per editor has risen more than fourfold.
Retail Express
Retail Express has transformed grocery pricing by replacing manual, error-prone spreadsheets with an AI powered Intelligent Merchandising engine. Focused on Pricing Automation and Automatic Application of Retailer Strategy, the solution elevates trading teams from administrative roles to strategic leaders.
By automating routine pricing actions across the long tail, ensuring strict guardrails, margin protection, and compliance - the platform powers real-time responses to cost changes and competitor moves. Deployed with a major European grocer, the solution achieved an 85% automation rate, boosted gross margin by 2%, and cut competitor response times from two weeks to two minutes.
Snag and Patchworks
Snag, a size inclusive DTC fashion brand shipping to 100+ countries, has taken AI beyond chat and into live retail operations.
Using Claude as the reasoning layer and Patchworks as the execution layer via MCP, Snag's team now runs product and order operations across multiple Shopify storefronts, five warehouse systems, its PLM, Sage 200 and marketplaces through plain language instructions.
Patchworks closed the gaps native AI connectors couldn't: it reached systems with no MCP server and unlocked Shopify's Bulk Operations API. The result: 14,000+ products updated in a single operation, and one of Snag's fastest ever product launches, delivered in around two weeks.

items.body:
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Best Data Analytics Driven Retail Initiative finalists announced
We’re pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Best Data Analytics Driven Retail Initiative category. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector.
Check out a rundown of our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.

Our 2026 Best Data Analytics Driven Retail Initiative finalists as follows:
Circana
Circana's data science team built Demand Forecaster, a self-correcting forecasting system run as a two-level tournament. Demand drivers compete for a place in each model, then forecasting methods compete to project each driver, with every round decided by explicit, auditable rules.
Built in Circana Unify+, it forecasts in each retailer's own hierarchy, from total store to SKU/UPC, across edible, non-edible and general merchandise. Retailers progress from ad hoc projects to annual contracts, multi-year agreements and direct tool access. Multiple retailers are now signed up for multi-year engagements, and adoption has grown from a handful to many of the world's largest.
Datitude
Retail data is fragmented by design. Tech stacks built around systems/tools, each with its own version of the truth. Datitude's unified retail data platform solves that problem at source. Five connected layers integrate, clean, model, define and surface data, giving every team access to the same trusted numbers through Datitude's Application, Excel Add-in, BI tools, data feeds and now, AI.
New this year is a Semantic Layer and AI Gateway, extending the governed foundation for advanced analytics to AI. One platform connecting, integrating and unifying data. More data, more use cases, more ways to access it. Better, trusted intelligence.
EE Retail
Own Your Town transforms complex customer, commercial, geographic and retail data into actionable local intelligence. By connecting previously separate datasets, every EE store can understand the size of the opportunity within its catchment, how much it is capturing and where future growth lies.
Instead of simply reporting past performance, the initiative gives store leaders clear insight into where to focus their teams next. The result is a powerful connection between national growth strategy and frontline action, supporting EE's ambition to grow broadband net additions and already contributing to increased local ownership and market share. It shifts retail analytics from explaining yesterday to shaping tomorrow.
Focal Systems and Village Super Market
An empty shelf often isn't a true out-of-stock. The product is in a case overhead, and the store's systems can't say where. Focal Systems' Top Stock, launched in August 2026, closes that gap with data the store already collects.
Cameras installed in the store read coded labels on overhead cases every hour. Focal matches what they see against the store's inventory records and the gaps on the shelf below, then turns each match into a restocking task. In its first month at Village Super Market's ShopRite, Top Stock found $24,000 of inventory the store owned but couldn't see.
Footasylum and invent.ai
As Footasylum strategically expanded its UK bricks and mortar network, growing complexity across forecasting, demand planning and inter-branch transfers was creating operational inefficiencies and impacting product availability.
The retailer partnered with invent.ai to overhaul its forecasting and inventory processes, replacing manual inventory rules with automated, data driven decisioning. Invent.ai’s AI decisioning platform turns retail data into automated decisions and actions, enabling Footasylum to forecast demand more accurately and automatically execute optimal inventory decisions at SKU and store level.
HyperFinity and JD Sports
Personalisation is easy to promise and hard to prove. JD Sports wanted proof before committing further budget to a loyalty programme. So HyperFinity built it a centralised personalisation engine and ran three controlled trials: category offers, spend-based incentives, cross-sell mechanics. Each trial answered one question at a time.
The result: a 3.2% uplift in in-store loyalty sales, plus dashboards, segmentations and campaign templates JD's team now run themselves. The learnings are now shaping how JD evolves its personalisation strategy.
MRI Software and Sky
Sky partnered with MRI Software to transform how it measures customer engagement across its retail estate, particularly its mid-mall concessions where traditional footfall metrics fall short.
Using MRI’s footfall analytics solution, Sky can capture visitor volumes, movement and engagement around these open retail environments, creating a 360-degree view of customer behaviour. The initiative turns previously difficult-to-measure interactions into actionable intelligence, enabling Sky to compare performance across different retail formats and better understand demand and conversion.
Quorso and Currys
Currys operates 296 stores across the UK and Ireland, and like most large format retailers, it had more data than its store teams could act on. Reports arrived across multiple platforms and took hours each week to work through.
Regional averages also hid what each store actually needed. Working with Quorso, Currys launched Action AI. It unifies data from every source, in whatever format it arrives, and analyses each store individually to surface the specific actions most likely to move its numbers.
A focused proof of concept on sales and customer satisfaction delivered uplift on both, including a £20-40 million sales uplift in the first year. Action AI achieved 100% General Manager engagement from day one and has reallocated around five hours per store per week from reporting to the shop floor.
Retail Express
Retail Express partnered with a leading regional UK convenience store operator (240+ stores, £147 million+ 12-week turnover) to transform how raw transaction, margin, and competitor pricing data is unified and acted upon.
Leveraging the Retail Express Intelligent Merchandising platform, the initiative deployed AI driven volumetric product analytics (ABC classification), granular store demographic profiling, and competitor price matching. By replacing fragmented, manual systems with algorithmic rules-based pricing, the platform enables real-time decision-making, unlocking a £3.98 million annualised profit opportunity (+100 bps margin expansion) while sharpening customer price perception on essential everyday items.
Vusion and Kavanagh
Vusion360 brings together the full suite of Vusion’s technologies, transforming the store into a fully connected, intelligent and data driven ecosystem.
Electronic shelf labels, EdgeSense, Captana, Pulse, VusionLive and VusionCloud each work in tandem to turn data from across the store into practical and actionable insights for retailers. The system enables prices and promotions to be updated in real-time, constant shelf monitoring and expiry management, and the ability to communicate and display a wealth of product information right at the shelf edge.
Kavanagh’s Belsize Park became the UK’s first store to be fully equipped with Vusion360. The initiative connects and analyses store data, enabling Kavanagh’s to identify and resolve issues faster and make better-informed decisions that improve operations and reduce waste, all while continuing to deliver a high quality shopping experience for their customers.

Our 2026 Global AI Technology finalists as follows:
Logile and Vallarta Supermarkets
Vallarta Supermarkets transformed fresh operations with Logile’s AI powered Fresh Operations Management capabilities, connecting item level forecasting, production, inventory, labour and store execution.
Advanced AI and machine learning models continuously learn and adapt to demand signals, helping teams determine what to produce, when to produce it and the resources needed to execute. Automated workflows turn intelligence into daily action across stores.
Independent analysis by Nucleus Research found a 1,070% ROI, 15.2-month payback and more than $10.6 million in attributable profit over three years. Vallarta also reduced software costs 15% while increasing sales across multiple fresh departments.
My Instore Radio
AI Voices by My Instore Radio enhances how retailers and hospitality businesses create and manage in-store communication. In one browser-based workflow, a built-in AI assistant helps users write and refine a message, after which they can select the language, regional variant, voice, style and speaking speed, add background music, preview the final mix and schedule it by location, date, day and time.
Announcements that traditionally required external voice talent, recording and production can now be created and deployed in minutes. The solution is already used across multiple markets for promotions, opening hours, service announcements and other time-sensitive communication.
Profitmind
Retailers need to understand how their assortments, prices and promotions compare with the competition. Profitmind developed Awase, an AI model that matches products across retailers so merchants can see where they overlap and where there are gaps worth pursuing.
Built with feedback from experienced merchandisers, Awase supports competitive analysis when shared product codes are unavailable or inconsistent. It produced 61% fewer first-attempt matching errors than the strongest retail specific alternative tested. In production with Profitmind customers since April 2026, Awase gives retailers a clearer view of their market position to guide pricing and assortment decisions that support their own strategy.
Screenix
Screenix created an AI fashion avatar that brings the intelligence of online retail into the physical store. Shown on a spatial 3D display, the avatar presents the latest collection and catches shoppers' attention. All content is produced with generative AI, so a retailer can refresh looks quickly without a new photoshoot for every campaign.
Live in a fashion store, it is the first AI powered spatial display installation in Benelux fashion retail. The project shows how AI can be used next to employees to give customers more inspiration and gives retailers a repeatable model for connected in-store experiences. On top of that the relevant clothes are displayed next to the screen and the full look can be bought immediately.
Sphere
Sphere deployed an AI powered inventory optimisation solution for a $200 million B2B distributor serving the retail supplies market. The system unified CRM data, customer behavior, sales history and real-time market signals from Amazon, eBay and competitor pricing. It then generated recommendations for inventory selection, vendor negotiations, pricing, customer targeting and demand forecasting.
The result was an 85% faster decision cycle, 10% higher gross margins, 30% lower operational costs and a 25% increase in repeat buyers. Within 12 months, annual revenue grew from $200 million to $250 million, demonstrating AI delivering measurable value at scale.
Sitoo
Sitoo SIA brings AI support into Sitoo POS and BackOffice, giving retailers 24/7 access to Sitoo knowledge in more than 40 languages.
When SIA can answer the question, it provides an immediate response. When human expertise is needed, it can connect the user with the appropriate Sitoo support or product expert. SIA resolves more than 60% of the conversations it handles, with customer satisfaction at almost 90%. Retailers including Gina Tricot and Paul Smith show how SIA is creating value in different ways, from faster support to helping store teams learn the system.
Slive.ai
Slive.ai unifies three layers usually sold as separate products: a modular business engine spanning store, sales, items, purchasing, warehouse and treasury; a native collaborative network where every conversation is anchored to the transaction it concerns; and a team of AI agents led by Astro Slive that execute operations rather than merely answering questions.
Elena watches inventory, Vera reads sales, Nick prepares purchasing and Sophi manages collections, and no agent acts without the owner's approval. Its App Store lets each company activate only what it needs and scale module by module. Launched commercially in November 2025 by Bigwise Corp, Slive.ai has grown cumulative adoption over 380% since launch.
TCS
TCS Optumera is an agentic AI powered merchandising platform that leverages artificial intelligence built on all major machine learning paradigms including supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, and reinforcement learning, enabling the platform to sense, reason, simulate, and optimise continuously across pricing, assortment and space.
The platform continuously listens to market, competitive, and environmental signals; anticipates demand shifts; and recommends precise, profitable actions across merchandising functions. During sudden changes such as a weather event or a competitor promotion, Optumera autonomously senses the shift, forecasts impact, and proposes optimised pricing, space realignments, and updated assortments, converting disruption into advantage.

Morrisons taps Logile to enhance store planning across supermarket, convenience, logistics sites
Morrisons has selected Logile as it looks to enhance store workload planning across the UK grocery retailer’s business. The agreement covers its supermarket and convenience store estate alongside its logistics network.
Morrisons is implementing Logile software in a bid to simplify central planning, replacing time-consuming manual spreadsheets with optimised operational data and intelligence. By delivering clearer visibility into store workload requirements, it says that central operations can provide accurate, reliable insight across the estate, allowing teams to focus on better supporting store operations.
“Getting colleagues where customers need them most is the heart of what we do, and at our scale you need a reliable, shared foundation to get that right,” says Alex Rose, Head of Productivity at Morrisons. “A large supermarket and a local convenience store operate differently so our planning has to flex to those local needs while keeping central support consistent. When our store managers have plans they can depend on, they spend less time managing admin and more time supporting their colleagues and serving customers.”
The roll-out starts with Logile’s Enterprise Standards Manager, which sets a central definition of the work each operation requires, alongside its workload planning tools, which turn store tasks into clear, accurate operational requirements. Operational and store planning modules carry these requirements into day-to-day planning, while Enterprise Performance Dashboards give all levels of the business a view of store operations across the estate. Logile will deliver the programme in collaboration with its partner FrontlineXP.
“UK grocers are increasingly focused on effectively supporting workload planning and operations, and the ones making progress start by agreeing on what the work actually is,” says James Freshwater, Vice President, UK EMEA & International at Logile. “Morrisons is doing that across its entire estate, from its largest supermarkets to its logistics sites, and that takes conviction from the top. Our part is to make that foundation accurate and simple for their teams to use every day, so the value shows up on the shopfloor and in the warehouse.”

items.title: Mark Kleinman: Every Lidl helps a new era of supermarket mergers

For that matter, every Aldi does too. With apologies to the creators of Tesco’s famous advertising slogan, that might be the neatest way to encapsulate [...]
items.body:
Mark Kleinman: Every Lidl helps a new era of supermarket mergers
Mark Kleinman is Sky News’ City editor and the man who gets the Square Mile talking in his City AM column.
Every Lidl helps a new era of supermarket mergers
Every Lidl helps. For that matter, every Aldi does too. With apologies to the creators of Tesco’s famous advertising slogan, that might be the neatest way to encapsulate the ambitions of its rivals to spark a new wave of consolidation in Britain’s grocery retail industry.
Not much more than a decade on from its own near-death experience, triggered by an accounting scandal which left the country’s biggest supermarket chain racing to secure an emergency warchest, Tesco’s status as the market supremo has rarely looked so firmly entrenched.
This partly explains why J Sainsbury, in a distant second place as measured by Kantar’s market share data, held preliminary merger conversations with smaller rival Morrisons earlier this year, as I revealed on Sky News last week. According to the FT, it was Sainsbury’s which then terminated the discussions.
There’s good reason to believe, though, that this represented a mere pause, rather than a final halt to negotiations over a combination bringing together any two of Asda, Morrisons and Sainsbury’s. If anything, the impetus for a transaction has strengthened, rather than dissipated, since that last round of discussions: heightened food insecurity, growing anxiety about employment costs – fuelled by Rachel Reeves’ 2024 Budget and not alleviated since – and persistent pressure from ministers (some of which has been subtle, some not) on UK competition regulators to be ‘pro-growth’ all point towards a greater likelihood of a deal being stitched together.
It’s not without irony that the emergence of discounters Aldi and Lidl as formidable players in a sector previously regarded as impenetrable to outsiders is a major contributor to the fact that a deal between two of the big guns is now more plausible than when Sainsbury’s and Asda tried to come together in 2018.
Whether Sainsbury’s is a participant this time around is an open question. Chief executive Simon Roberts needs to revive a meaningful growth story for his investors and he cannot afford to be left behind by his two closest rivals coming together. The same, though, can be said for both Asda and Morrisons, and their private equity owners.
Will BT conclude that it’s still good to TalkTalk?
It’s good to talk, went the old BT advertising campaign featuring Maureen Lipman, but is it good to TalkTalk? That’s the question facing BT Group and its shareholders after last week’s rescue of the company founded by Sir Charles Dunstone in 2004.
TalkTalk’s cost base and regulatory framework proved a toxic cocktail, which, ironically, meant that Openreach’s owner was its only logical saviour. BT hasn’t half played the role of a reluctant paramour, though. Its entreaties to government to alleviate the competition risks attached to a takeover came at the eleventh hour, and even then the company let it be known that it didn’t really want to absorb TalkTalk’s retail customer base and its wholesale arm, PXC.
The irony of the antitrust waiver request won’t have been lost on Sir Charles, who occupied a role on the HBOS board when Gordon Brown’s government allowed Lloyds TSB’s rescue of the ailing bank to sail through in 2008.
People close to BT argue that a request from Epiris, the private equity firm which wanted to buy PXC, to write off its existing debt and give it three months’ rent-free use of its infrastructure – a package worth over £300m – meant the only rational alternative was to buy TalkTalk itself.
In the end, whether or not you agree that BT held the government and TalkTalk’s other stakeholders to hostage, the BT chief executive Allison Kirkby and her board played a shrewd hand to secure a strategic asset on the cheap – with one caveat. A protracted and messy legal battle, allied with a competition review which restokes the debate about BT Group’s structure (and in particular its ownership of Openreach), is itself fraught with reputational risk. There’s more TalkTalking to be done yet.
State of the Game report ushers New Deal talks into injury time
What a state. This week’s publication of the Independent Football Regulator’s (IFR) assessment of the health of the English game is as much a moral judgement as a financial one. How, it tacitly asks, can a professional sport envied around the world operate with 94 per cent of its clubs lossmaking and an even-higher percentage trading with negative EBITDA (ie with their core operating expenses higher than their total revenues)?
The watchdog’s answer, rightly, is that an industry which relies on the bulk of its owners frequently providing sufficient liquidity to ensure that employees get their salaries just hours before payroll is clearly unsustainable.
The IFR’s diagnosis of the problem is, therefore, on the money. In recent months, it has attempted to broker negotiations between the Premier League and English Football League, with only limited success. As I revealed on Sky News last week, while the top flight’s clubs have indicated that they might support a £180m-a-year solidarity payments offer if they receive assurances of approval by the EFL, the lower leagues’ chair, Rick Parry, has been holding out for annual payments of £207m.
Premier League clubs have little appetite to accede to that request, which effectively returns the entire process to the limbo-like state in which it has existed for most of the last three years. Injury time beckons, in every sense.

items.body:
Panic on the streets of Nottingham: GMB union slams Deliveroo and Coco Robotics delivery robots trial
The GMB union, which represents couriers across Deliveroo's rider network, has hit out at the quick commerce company’s trial of delivery robots on Nottingham streets. As reported by RTIH earlier this month, these are supplied by US company Coco and will be used for takeaways and groceries, with Deliveroo claiming that there are no plans to replace human riders but rather the move complements them during off peak hours.
Canary Wharf, Milton Keynes, Leeds, Stockton-on-Tees, and Nottingham are the initial areas to get the service, with plans afoot for a broader UK roll-out.
Deliveroo runs a three-sided marketplace across roughly restaurants, grocers and retailers, all promising delivery in as little as 30 minutes. It is also a DoorDash subsidiary now, after being taken over by the US giant in a deal valuing the business at £2.9 billion. So this move shouldn’t come as a huge surprise.
Claude Bahati, GMB Organiser, says: "If Deliveroo can afford to invest in autonomous technology, why can it not invest properly in the workers who keep the platform running every day? Innovation should not come at the expense of real people, and these developments must always be negotiated with workers.”
He adds: "It is disappointing that engagement from Deliveroo or the Mayor has not been forthcoming. Food couriers continue to struggle with rising living costs and are calling for fairer pay and compensation for return journeys. At the same time, many riders face poor treatment at work, often being forced to wait outside in all weather conditions without being given access to the facilities and support needed to do their job.”
"Decision makers must pay greater attention to the realities of the gig economy and ensure that riders are treated with dignity, respect and fairness. Deliveroo’s future must include investment in the people who have built its success, not just it's technologies."
Deliveroo did not respond to our request for comment.

2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Sustainable Retail finalists include Morrisons, Minimist, and Pricer

Our 2026 Sustainable Retail Innovation finalists as follows:
Gatekeeper Systems and Morrisons
Gatekeeper Systems and Morrisons have partnered to deploy intelligent trolley retention technology across high-risk stores, demonstrating that loss prevention and sustainability are complementary goals.
The Cart Control programme uses prevention first, wheel locking systems to keep trolleys within store car park perimeters. An initial five-store efficacy trial delivered a 67% reduction in trolley losses, avoiding an estimated 87.4 tonnes of CO₂e annually, equivalent to removing 20 petrol cars from UK roads. The programme has since expanded to 19 stores with further roll-outs planned, proving this is a scalable, replicable innovation with measurable environmental and commercial impact across the grocery retail sector.
Minimist
Every donated item that fails to sell is goods heading for export or landfill. Around 1 to 3% of charity retail stock is listed online, so the sector's unsold volume is enormous and largely invisible.
Minimist makes listing donated items faster than not listing them, which puts stock in front of buyers who want it. 28 charity retailers have listed 73,844 items and sold 31,580, avoiding 197.6 tonnes of CO2e net and keeping 44.6 tonnes of material out of landfill and incineration, while raising 1,409,994 euros. The impact measures are an annex to Minimist's shareholder agreement with Tilia Impact Ventures and the reporting right is legally binding.
Pricer and Company Shop Group
Pricer and Company Shop Group have transformed the shelf edge across the UK’s leading Company Shop ‘Surplus Supermarket’ estate, using electronic shelf labels (ESLs) and automated pricing to help more surplus food find a home rather than go to waste.
As a surplus redistributor, Company Shop has to deal with rapidly changing, short shelf-life products which can require multiple price changes daily to ensure the stock is sold and not wasted. Pricer’s centrally controlled ESLs replace labour intensive manual updates with accurate, real time pricing and markdowns help maximise sell-through while protecting Company Shop’s value proposition.
The solution has contributed to a 5% improvement in productivity, freeing colleagues for customer facing tasks while supporting Company Shop’s mission to ensure no surplus product goes to waste.
SharkNinja and Ingram Micro Lifecycle
Since 2022, SharkNinja and Ingram Micro Lifecycle have built a circular economy programme for small domestic appliances, now supporting more than 900 SKUs across Europe and North America and giving a second life to over 83% of returned products.
Through advanced repair, refurbishment, parts harvesting, and recommerce, the programme maximises product recovery, reduces e-waste, and lowers demand for virgin materials. Refurbished products are resold through major consumer channels, generating new revenue while increasing access to affordable, sustainable appliances.
Engineering insights from returns data improve product quality, repairability, and future design, while faster processing enhances customer experience and warranty resolution.

items.body:
As Morrisons tests Instacart smart trolleys research finds that many Brits distrust the tech behind them
28% of UK consumers do not trust artificial intelligence in retail at all, as retailers such as Morrisons introduce new technology to the weekly shop, according to research from e-commerce marketing platform Omnisend.
The company surveyed 1,086 Brits for this. 29% are concerned that AI will lead to job losses on the high street. 27% feel their activity is being tracked by supermarkets, while 53% believe loyalty schemes such as Tesco Clubcard and Sainsbury's Nectar monitor their spending habits. The findings come as Morrisons trials Instacart's AI powered Caper smart trolleys at a Preston store, becoming the first UK retailer to introduce the technology. Elsewhere, Lidl extended its Lidl & Go trial to another 37 stores during July, allowing customers to scan products through the Lidl Plus app and track their spending and savings in real-time
55% of respondents have used a scan-as-you-shop device in a supermarket. Among those who have tried the technology, 70% used it to save time at the checkout, while 24% tapped it to help stick to a budget. A further 5% wanted to reduce the amount of interaction they had with supermarket staff. Just 8% of all respondents said scan-as-you-shop devices make them feel as though their every move is being tracked, while 20% said the technology makes their weekly shop more efficient.
Marty Bauer, E-commerce Expert at Omnisend, comments: "Saving time and keeping track of spending are clear reasons for shoppers to use self-scanning. But retailers should not assume that familiarity with a handheld scanner translates into trust in AI. They need to explain what these new tools do, what information they use and how customers benefit.”
"Concerns about potential job losses deserve an answer too. Retailers should explain how staff roles will change and make sure help remains easy to find. A quicker shop loses its appeal if customers cannot find someone to resolve a problem. Smart trolleys bring product recommendations directly into the supermarket aisle, giving retailers another opportunity to influence buying decisions. That makes the quality of those suggestions important. A relevant offer can be welcome, but repeatedly encouraging shoppers to add more could undermine the appeal of a tool they use to stay within budget.”
He adds: "For shoppers, the running total can help them keep an eye on spending, but a personalised offer is not automatically the best deal. Check unit prices, compare alternatives and ask whether you actually need the recommended item. It is also worth reviewing the privacy and marketing choices available in any linked loyalty app. Retailers should judge success by whether customers want to use the technology again, as well as what they spend. Clear information, useful recommendations and a choice of checkout options can help build that confidence."

items.body:
Former Kount CEO Brad Wiskirchen joins chargeback prevention and remediation tech firm Chargebacks911
Chargebacks911, a specialist in chargeback processing and dispute management technology, has announced the appointment of Brad Wiskirchen, former CEO at Kount, as its new Chief Commercial Officer (CCO), and also CEO at its financial institution focused sister brand, Fi911.
Wiskirchen will spearhead strategic M&A initiatives, pursue high value partnerships and expand relationships with financial institutions, payment processors and payment orchestration providers worldwide.
“Brad’s appointment is about more than expanding our leadership team. It’s about accelerating what’s next,” says Monica Eaton, Founder and CEO at Chargebacks911. “We’ve spent years building the technology, infrastructure and industry relationships that have positioned Chargebacks911 at the center of an increasingly important part of the payments ecosystem. The opportunities ahead extend well beyond traditional dispute management, and we're bringing together the talent, capabilities and strategic relationships to pursue them at scale.”
In addition to being founding CEO at Kount, Wiskirchen also served as an industrial partner at CVC Capital Partners, a private equity and investment firm, where he led FinTech investment efforts in North America. Additionally, Wiskirchen was named Chairman of the Salt Lake City Branch of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, as well as a member of the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) Interdepartmental Working Group on Finance and Technology, High-Level Advisory Group.
Wiskirchen has also served on numerous for-profit and non-profit boards in the payments, fraud, identity and compliance spaces, and has co-founded and invested in various businesses in those spaces.
"Brad has unmatched entrepreneurial acumen, understands the investment landscape and brings the commercial instincts and relationships to help us capitalise on opportunities that can meaningfully expand our reach,” says Benjamin Bridwell, President at Chargebacks911. “We're not simply looking to grow our existing business. We're looking to reshape what's possible across the payments ecosystem."
“What Monica and the team have built is remarkable, and I see enormous potential in what comes next. I haven’t seen a more impressive foundation of technology, industry connectivity and market reach,” says Wiskirchen. “I've spent my career building and scaling technology companies, and it's rare to find a business with this combination of proprietary technology, established market reach and opportunity for expansion.”
“Chargebacks911 has already built the foundation. Now we have an opportunity to dramatically accelerate its scale through strategic acquisitions, new partnerships and expansion into adjacent markets. The convergence of AI, payments intelligence and financial services is creating extraordinary opportunities, and I believe Chargebacks911 is uniquely positioned to capitalise on them. I'm excited to work alongside Monica and the leadership team to help build the next chapter of this company's success.”

It reads all of it to determine which campaigns to run next, then builds the work itself: the calendar, the content, the approvals and the team handoffs that used to happen by hand.
"Every tool in a brand's stack is getting AI, but each one only sees its own corner of the business," says Jessica Herrin, Founder and CEO at Marklo (who previously founded Stella & Dot Brands). "Great merchants don't work that way. You can't decide what to market next without knowing what sold, what's in stock, what you've already promoted, what's coming, and what the rest of your category is doing. Marklo sees all of it, spots the next opportunity and gets the work moving."
Marklo connects the tools brands already use - Shopify, Klaviyo, Attentive, Meta, Google, Canva, Figma and more - so products, inventory, promotions, campaigns, creative and results all sit in one system. Once connected, it reconstructs launches, promotions, email, SMS, paid media, social activity and revenue into a day-by-day, year-over-year marketing calendar, with the aim of giving teams an immediate view of what drove sales and what was happening around it.
"We already had Shopify, Klaviyo and analytics tools. What was missing was one place that connected all of our marketing campaigns, inventory and sales data," says Allison Plaisance, Senior Director of Retention Marketing at Away. "Marklo gives us the whole commercial picture and an actionable path forward."
"One of the most pervasive shifts in startup formation over the past few years is leaner teams doing more with less. Intelligence changed the equation for how builders can bring products to life, and market and scale them," says Kirsten Green, Founding Partner at Forerunner. "Consumer brands are some of the businesses that stand to benefit from this most. Jessica understands this opportunity deeply, as she spent 20 years building breakout brands and is a genuine expert on how AI can better drive and accelerate the marketing funnel."
Marklo will use the funding to grow its product and engineering teams, expand its public beta and invest in customer success and community programmes.
"Most brands are running cross-channel marketing out of a patchwork of spreadsheets, decks and ten different logins," says Herrin. "I've been lucky to build with great merchandising, creative and business intelligence teams, and even then, the hardest part was getting everyone working from the same picture. Marklo gives every marketer that picture and does the assembly work around it, whether the team is two people or twenty, so they can make smarter decisions, move faster and stop leaving revenue and margin on the table."
