items.body:
Plan Black Friday as a five-week peak: this is what two years of shipping data show
Six in ten of the extra shipments in peak season go out in the weeks before and after Black Friday. Planning for all five weeks means spreading carrier capacity and staff, and keeping checkout settings easy to change.
Peak season is a five-week job for carriers, warehouses and checkout teams. On the nShift platform, Black Friday carries more than twice the shipments of an ordinary Friday in early November, two years running, yet in both 2024 and 2025 most of the shipments above an average early-November week went out before or after Black Week, the Monday-to-Sunday week around Black Friday.
The figures cover outbound shipments across our whole platform, from late October to the end of December.
Agree extra carrier capacity for every week of the peak
In 2025 the week after Black Week still stood at 1.47 times an average early November week and accounted for a quarter of the extra shipments. The peak lasted about five weeks that year, from 17th November to 21st December. Black Week itself (24th to 30th November) peaked at 1.74 times the average and carried 40% of the extra shipments, while the week before carried 14%.
2024 followed almost the same pattern, and the week-by-week figures for both years are on our Black Friday hub. I would agree daily collection numbers with each carrier for all five weeks, with Black Week and the week after it as the two heaviest.
Plan Black Week Saturday like a weekday
On Black Week Saturday in 2025, shipments came to four times an ordinary Saturday and reached 90.8% of an ordinary Tuesday, because weekend volumes start low. The Sunday was 2.8 times an ordinary Sunday. I would give that Saturday weekday staffing and weekday carrier collections, especially in a warehouse that normally runs a light weekend shift.
Two days later, Cyber Monday was the busiest day of the 2025 season, with 8% more shipments than Black Friday, partly because Mondays carry more shipments than Fridays throughout the year. I would book the season’s largest carrier collections for that Monday.
Forecast each sending country separately
In Black Week 2025, shipments sent from the UK rose 112% above an average week, the highest of seven nShift sending markets, against 44% for shipments from Finland. Using one uplift figure for every country would have under-planned UK volumes, so build the forecast country by country, starting from your own campaign calendar.
Your own campaigns can create sharper peaks
Finnish retailer Stockmann, which runs nShift Checkout, holds its Crazy Days campaign twice a year, and on those days morning orders can jump to around 30 times a normal day. Through the surge, its checkout processes 2,000+ checkout API calls per minute. “If the checkout cannot handle this load, the success of the entire campaign is at risk,” says Jari Reinikainen, Logistics Director at Stockmann.
Stockmann’s logistics team can also adjust delivery methods while the sale is running: if a carrier runs into problems, the team can switch that method off in about 30 seconds. The customer story explains how Stockmann keeps checkout stable at that volume.
Make mid-peak changes in settings
Carrier capacity, integrations and major checkout changes may need months to arrange, so start with those. During the peak, you will adjust the rest of the plan as volumes come in: delivery offers that start and end with a campaign, a carrier option paused if its service becomes unreliable and return windows set for gifts. Your team can usually make these changes close to the date, as long as they are settings it controls.
Our experts show how to make them in a 30-minute live session on peak settings, following one Black Friday order from checkout to return and changing its delivery and returns rules in nShift, without a developer.
About the author
Jacob Hopewell is a Logistics and Retail Software Consultant at nShift, the global leader in multi-carrier shipping and delivery experience. He works with UK retailers and brands on delivery across checkout, shipping, tracking and returns. The nShift platform connects to over 1,000 carriers and supports over one billion shipments a year.

items.title: Retailers back on alert after new wave of cyber attacks
items.summary: When Asos customers were sent a cryptically-worded push notification on Tuesday last week, some shoppers thought they were being hawked the fast fashion retailer’s new Christmas collection.  One thought the alert was “some crappy marketing scheme to get me to check the app and to view their snowflake collection,” they wrote on X. The notification [...]
items.body:
Retailers back on alert after new wave of cyber attacks
When Asos customers were sent a cryptically-worded push notification on Tuesday last week, some shoppers thought they were being hawked the fast fashion retailer’s new Christmas collection.
One thought the alert was “some crappy marketing scheme to get me to check the app and to view their snowflake collection,” they wrote on X. The notification was in fact a direct threat to Asos’s management, threatening to leak information belonging to the company’s millions of customers.
The hackers say they gained access to Asos’s servers on Snowflake, a cloud platform service which allows retailers to store basic customer information and send push notifications.
Asos has tried to reassure customers that no payment information was stolen and that the app remains safe to use, but the group behind the incident have claimed the data breach was worse than the London-listed company is making out.
Days later, high street retailer H&M said it was investigating claims that Shinyhunters, a global criminal hacking group which is currently being pursued by the FBI, had hacked into its servers.
The Foschini Group (TFG), the Johannesburg-listed retail group which owns fashion brands like White Stuff, said on Tuesday that it was aware of a “cybersecurity incident” at its London business.
The firm said the IT systems and websites of some of its brands – including Phase Eight, Hobbs and Whistles – were impacted, adding that there was “no reason to believe that payment information is at risk”.
‘Unprecedented’ attack on French grocers
On the continent, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize was forced to shut down several systems following a “security issue” on its network.
Separately, fridges at a number of French supermarket chains were hit with a hack which forced them to warm up to as high as 50C, spoiling fresh and frozen food said to be worth millions of euros.
Dominique Schelcher, chief executive of grocery chain Coopérative U, said the incident “is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented”.
Tech experts said this attack is of particular concern because they suggest that future cyber incidents could threaten food security.
“Hackers don’t need to get into the tills to cause havoc in a supermarket,” said Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at online services provider NordVPN.
“Interfere with the equipment keeping food cold and you can force stores to throw away valuable stock, shut entire aisles and leave shoppers facing empty fridges and freezers. A cyberattack can quickly become a food safety problem, as well as a very expensive one for retailers.”
This latest wave of retail cyber attacks comes less than two years after Co-op, Marks and Spencer and Harrods were hit with data breaches in spring of last year. These retailers are still recovering, with Co-op saying the incident cost it £206m in revenue.
Tesco ‘constantly vigilant’
Retailers are keen to ensure that they are not the next target. Aim-listed toys and crafts seller The Works contacted its staff the day after the Asos breach to remind them to be vigilant for attempts, it is understood.
Speaking in the days following the attack, Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy said the supermarket was watching the Asos incident closely in the hopes of learning how to avoid being the next victim.
He said: “We invest very, very heavily in cybersecurity. It’s something we take exceptionally seriously for obvious reasons. We’re constantly vigilant.”
Murphy added that the UK’s biggest grocer was “staying up to date” with the latest prevention methods and updating its employees on how to avoid cyber attacks.
“We will obviously seek to learn from any incident, including the Asos incident, to make sure that we are staying on top of that,” he said.
Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, said UK retailers spend hundreds of millions of pounds every year on their cyber defences. “Cyber-attacks are a very real risk for all businesses and are becoming increasingly sophisticated,” she said.
While FTSE 100 firms like Tesco can easily pile cash into shoring up their cyber defences with complex systems, cyber attacks often rely on old-fashioned human error.
Asos’s hackers gained access to its Snowflake systems by posing as a “trusted contact” of an employee to obtain their login information. The attacks on M&S and Co-op began in a similar way, as IT workers were tricked into giving away their credentials.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said this latest wave of cyber attacks will serve as a “brutal alarm call” for retailers.
“Retailers are particularly attractive targets, sitting on valuable customer data and relying on interconnected systems to keep everything from online orders to supply chains moving,” she said.
“The consequences of a breach can stretch far beyond stolen information, hitting sales, disrupting operations and eroding customer trust.”

items.title: How a Chinese-made toy gets to a US retailer
items.summary: With Christmas on the horizon, we trace children's toys from factories in China to US shelves.
items.body:
How a Chinese-made toy gets to a US retailer
- Published
On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words â "Made in China".
Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external
Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (Â£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external
With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.
As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.
The factory
Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.
In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.
The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.
Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.
Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."
Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.
So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.
On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.
Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.
Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.
He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."
And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.
Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report, external at the start of this year.
Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.
The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.
Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.
The ship
From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.
Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.
Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.
Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.
The US border
Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).
Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.
This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.
This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.
"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.
The US toy company
The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.
That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.
"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.
If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.
While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.
Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey.

Offering a popular […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Multi-format leisure destination GRID Braehead has welcomed local food brand Salt & Stacked. The opening marks the second food concept at GRID from the team behind Vinci’s, the brand’s sweet sister retailer that already operates at the destination, demonstrating confidence in GRID as a platform for independent operators to grow and develop.
Offering a popular mix of loaded fries and loaded mac, the arrival of Salt & Stacked supports GRID’s continued focus on developing a varied food and beverage offer that complements its retail, leisure and entertainment mix. Together, Salt & Stacked and Vinci’s provide visitors with decadent savoury and sweet options, helping to broaden customer choice and enhance the overall visitor experience.
The addition of a growing local independent alongside established brands, such as TGI Fridays, PizzaExpress and Nando’s, further strengthens GRID’s diverse dining mix, bringing together recognisable brands and homegrown concepts to create a more varied offer.
The opening also forms part of GRID’s wider strategy to create an all-day destination that encourages visitors to stay for longer and combine dining with shopping, leisure and entertainment. With food, drink, family attractions, outdoor retailers and activity-led operators all under one roof, GRID continues to strengthen its positioning as a destination day out with something for everyone.
Nicola Hiscoe, director of Salt & Stacked said: “GRID has proved to be a strong location for Salt & Stacked. As a well-established leisure destination, it gives us the platform to introduce the concept to a broad customer base, alongside a complementary mix of food, retail and entertainment. The response since launch has been extremely encouraging, giving us real confidence in Salt & Stacked’s potential to grow at GRID.”
Bruce Harley, centre manager at GRID Braehead, said: “Salt & Stacked is a strong addition to GRID and reflects the continued development of our food and beverage offer. The success of Vinci’s and the launch of this second concept demonstrates the opportunity here for operators to grow and respond to customer demand.
“As we continue to strengthen the mix of dining, leisure and retail at GRID, brands like Salt & Stacked extend customer choice and play an important role in building dwell time.”
For more information about Salt & Stacked, Vinci’s and GRID’s food and beverage offering, visit: https://gridbraehead.com/lets-dine/

The coffee chain, which operates over 600 cafes across the UK, said two new high-protein lattes would be rolled out across its entire estate in partnership with the THG-owned fitness brand. Neil Mistry, [...]
items.body:
Caffè Nero muscles into booming high-protein drinks market
Caffè Nero is looking to tap into the booming high-protein drinks market through a new deal with Manchester-based protein shake maker Myprotein.
The coffee chain, which operates over 600 cafes across the UK, said two new high-protein lattes would be rolled out across its entire estate in partnership with the THG-owned fitness brand.
Neil Mistry, boss of THG Nutrition, said there were growing signs that demand for protein coffee was coming across the Atlantic to the UK.
“Protein lattes have already taken off in the US, and we know the appetite is here too: our customers already add protein to their coffee at home,” said Neil Mistry, boss of THG Nutrition. “Now, with Caffè Nero, they can order it in a latte or matcha on the high street, across more than 600 stores.”
The two drinks, Iced Vanilla Protein Matcha Latte and the Iced Vanilla Protein Latte, are both under 160 calories and provide 24 grams of protein and 25 grams of protein, respectively.
Retailers and confectionary brands including Krispy Kreme, Mars and Snickers have struck deals with Myprotein in recent years in an effort to capitalise on booming for fitness-focused foods.
The global high protein food market was valued at $55.38bnin 2026 and is projected to grow to $105.34 billion by 2034, according to Fortune Business Insights.
Caffè Nero said it expects to roll-out more products under the partnership in January.
Lysa Hardy, boss of Caffè Nero UK, said the additions “respond to growing customer demand for high-protein drinks.”
THG Ingenuity, which was spun out of THG last year, is the owner of City AM.

items.body:
Available through The Wholesale Group’s independent wholesale members, Core Spring Water will be offered in 330ml and 500ml cartons, packed 24 per case, giving retailers a grab-and-go hydration option with environmental credentials.
The launch also marks another milestone for The Wholesale Group, with Core Spring Water becoming the first product in its own-brand portfolio to carry the B Corp logo following the Group’s recent achievement of B Corp Certification.

Tom Gittins, managing director – retail at The Wholesale Group, said: “Core Spring Water has been developed directly in response to member feedback and growing demand for a more sustainable alternative to conventional plastic bottled water.
“As our first own-brand water launch, it represents an important milestone for the Core range and demonstrates our commitment to delivering commercially relevant products that help our members respond to changing customer needs.

“Advance sales have been extremely strong, giving us confidence that there is genuine demand for this type of solution, and we look forward to seeing the range continue to grow.”

items.title: Poundland hits out at ‘speculation’ after union criticises owner
items.summary: Poundland has hit out at the “speculation” engulfing the company’s sale after a retail workers’ union dubbed its US owner an “absolute disgrace”.  Usdaw, the union representing shop workers, said earlier this week that it has “deep concerns” about US investment firm Gordon Brothers’s sale of the business.  Bally Auluk, Usdaw’s national officer, claimed Poundland’s [...]
items.body:
Poundland hits out at ‘speculation’ after union criticises owner
Poundland has hit out at the “speculation” engulfing the company’s sale after a retail workers’ union dubbed its US owner an “absolute disgrace”.
Usdaw, the union representing shop workers, said earlier this week that it has “deep concerns” about US investment firm Gordon Brothers’s sale of the business.
Bally Auluk, Usdaw’s national officer, claimed Poundland’s owner had refused to meet with the union, adding that the company is on the verge of falling into administration, putting 12,000 jobs at risk.
“With thousands of jobs on the line it is an absolute disgrace that Gordon Brothers has failed to engage with us to seek a secure future for the business,” he said.
“We are aware that a management buy-out has been attempted and we are told that their offers are being turned down.”
But it is understood that Poundland’s management repeatedly offered to meet with Usdaw and received no response. Sources close to the company said it would be highly unusual for a shareholders of a firm to meet with a union, even during a takeover process.
Usdaw’s suggestion that Gordon Brothers has refused a proposal by Poundland’s management to buy out the company is also understood to be incorrect.
Barry Williams, Poundland’s managing director, wrote to staff last week to tell them that press speculation over a management buyout option (MBO) was incorrect.
The retailer’s management had instead expressed a preference for one of the bidders and was working with them on their proposal, it is understood. This bidder is Martin Property Group, the Irish firm, which recently bought National Car Parks (NCP) out of administration.
A spokesperson for Poundland told City AM: “We understand these kinds of sale processes often lead to significant concern and speculation – much of it wide of the mark.
“We have always had an open door to Usdaw and they know we’re focused on the recovery that’s now firmly embedded in the business.”
Poundland sale gains pace
Usdaw said they still expect a meeting with Gordon Brothers. The union’s Auluk told City AM: “We are in constant contact with the management of Poundland, but it is the owners that are attempting to sell the business.
“When there is the potential for major changes, we would expect those responsible to fully engage with the staff through their trade union.”
Gordon Brothers kicked off its sale of Poundland last month, little more than a year after buying the company for a nominal £1 fee from retail group PepCo.
Advisors Alvarez & Marsal, who were appointed to run the sale, are weighing up bids from a number of buyers. These include proposals to carve up the business and offers for the entirety of the company.
Poundstretcher owner Fortress Investment Group and TG Jones owner Modella Capital are among the other parties who have expressed an interest in Poundland.
Gordon Brothers and Alvarez & Marsal declined to comment.

items.title: ACS announces new senior appointments to its board
items.summary: The Association of Convenience Stores (ACS) has made four new appointments to its board of directors from leading retail businesses in the convenience sector. The appointments are: Victoria Lockie, Head of Wholesale – acquisitions and strategic projects at Morrisons Kate McCrae, retail operations director at… This story continues at ACS announces new senior appointments to its board Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The appointments are:
- Victoria Lockie, Head of Wholesale – acquisitions and strategic projects at Morrisons
- Kate McCrae, retail operations director at The Co-operative Group
- Jerome Saint-Marc, managing director at Spar UK
- Dan Dixon, managing director, at William Reed
ACS chief executive Ed Woodall said: “We are delighted to welcome four new industry leaders to our Board, who bring a wealth of experience, fantastic insight and commitment to championing the convenience sector.
“These appointments will enhance and strengthen our ability to deliver the best representation, networking opportunities, and industry leading advice for ACS members.
“I would also like to take this opportunity to thank those who are moving on from their board positions for their continued, longstanding support of ACS and the work we do for local shops.”
ACS chairman and chief executive (integration) at Our Co-op, Phil Ponsonby said: “The appointment of four talented new directors further strengthens the ACS board, bringing a diverse range of skills and experience that will support our ongoing activity in representing convenience retailers.
“I’m looking forward to working with the new members of the board alongside existing directors to champion the role of ACS in the convenience sector.”
Victoria Lockie, who has over three decades of convenience retail experience in the independent sector through her current role at Morrisons and previous roles with Unitas and Nisa Retail, said: “I am delighted to be joining the ACS Board and look forward to bringing my experience to the opportunities and challenges facing our convenience retailers.
“It’s a privilege to be part of this Board having supported the ACS for many years, contributing to decisions that will help shape the future of the sector.”
Kate McCrae commented: “It’s a challenging time for food retailers, but local shops remain the backbone of their communities – providing access to food and other essentials, as well as creating job opportunities locally.
“ACS plays a vital role in championing convenience retailers, ensuring our voices are heard and that our concerns are acted upon, so I’m delighted to join its board at this pivotal moment.”
Jerome Saint-Marc, who was appointed the new managing director of Spar UK in August 2026, said: “I look forward to joining the ACS board, supporting the team and championing the convenience sector, working together through the ACS and its members to ensure the long-term sustainability of our sector.”
Dan Dixon, managing director, at William Reed, said: “It is a privilege to join the ACS board and contribute to an organisation that plays such an important role in supporting and representing the convenience sector.
“Convenience retail sits at the heart of local communities and continues to evolve at pace. I look forward to working alongside fellow board members to share insight, strengthen industry collaboration and help champion the long-term success of the sector.”

items.summary: Social media-driven craze puts ‘squishies’ up there with evergreen favourites such as Lego and Barbie, Hamleys says A cartoonish banana so addictively squidgy that it is “really difficult to put down” is tipped to be among the must-have toys this Christmas , according to expert buyers at Hamleys. items.body:
A cartoonish banana so addictively squidgy that it is “really difficult to put down” is tipped to be among the must-have toys this Christmas, according to expert buyers at Hamleys.
The £10 “slow-rise, squeezable, sensory” fruit taps into the “squishies” craze that is fuelling a high street boom in toy sales. In the coming weeks, Hamleys expects to sell thousands of the Big Squij toys, which come in a variety of food and animal shapes filled with a flour-based compound.
Their popularity has been supercharged by social media and a growing army of child and adult collectors. There are more than 260,000 TikTok posts and more than 600,000 on Instagram tagged #squishies. The most popular official brand, NeeDoh, has 1.1m TikTok followers.
Victoria Kay, the head of buying and merchandising at Hamleys, said the “squishy craze is only really just getting going”.
“The demand is huge. There is a wonderful simplicity to their power whether you are a young child or an adult. Literally once you squeeze one, it’s really difficult to put it down.”
Squishies are the biggest toy trend of the year, according to Andrew Murphy, who runs The Entertainer, the UK’s largest chain of toy shops. Some theories suggest their viral success is because of their stress-relieving powers or simplicity, but he suggests the “degree of fanaticism from kids under 10 for these products is not explainable in any rational way. It’s just a real, deep desire”.
The squishies craze is good news for independent toy shops, he said: “It will be increasing sales in total by minimum of 30%. Most of their costs are fixed so they’ll probably be doubling the profit for the year.”
The craze has been a shot in the arm for UK toy sales this year, which by the end of August were up 13% by value and 19% by volume, according the market research company Circana. Sales of toys that cost under £10 are growing fastest, with an extra £100m worth of these so-called “pocket money” items sold during the period thanks to the clamour for World Cup stickers and squishies.
As for Christmas – still 72 days away – Hamleys says this week is when shopping for the festive season “officially” starts, according to a poll of consumers. With that in mind it has produced its annual shortlist of toys to please toddlers through to teenagers and older. At £10, the Big Squij toys are the cheapest. while the remote-controlled flying Thunder Unicorn” is the most expensive at £75.
The list of 15 items includes evergreen favourites such as Lego, Barbie, Peppa Pig and PlayDoh. With the upcoming Marvel superhero extravaganza Avengers: Doomsday on the horizon it features two Doctor Doom toys – a £45 Lego bust and a £30 action figure.
There is also something for J-Pop fans with a collectible figurine of the computer-generated pop-star Hatsune Miku. The 16-year-old vocaloid – her “voice” comes from music software – is playing London’s O2 arena next month.

items.body:
Brits could be swapping sweet for bitter, turning beans into the main event and looking to their food cupboards for their next beauty fix in 2027, according to Whole Foods Market’s annual food and drink trend predictions for the UK.
The retailer’s Trends Council has identified eight trends it expects to shape how people shop, cook and eat over the year ahead – from the rise of “Beautrition”, where food and beauty increasingly collide, to a growing appetite for Japanese comfort food, intensely bitter flavours and premium beans and legumes.
Also on the agenda is a greater focus on where food comes from, simpler ingredient lists, reinvented versions of familiar dishes and a new wave of products designed to reduce waste – signalling a shift towards food that delivers on flavour, provenance, functionality and value.
The Whole Foods Market Trends Council – a collective of foragers, buyers and culinary experts – develops the predictions each year through industry experience, keen observation of consumer preferences, and long-standing relationships with emerging and established brands.
“This year’s predictions reflect a shift in how people are eating here in the UK. Customers are increasingly curious about where their food comes from, open to discovering new and reinvented flavours, and show an overall desire for simple, whole-food ingredients that deliver on both quality and taste. From the growing appetite for beans and legumes to Japanese-inspired comfort food and more complex bitter flavours, we’re seeing shoppers embrace a wider variety of ingredients and cuisines. At the same time, provenance and reducing waste continue to influence choices, showing that customers are thinking not only about what they eat, but where it comes from and how it is made,” shared Jade Hoai, Executive Lead of Purchasing, Whole Foods Market UK.
Whole Foods Market’s eight food trend trends to watch in 2027
The Bean Boom
Once relegated to side-dish status, beans and legumes are now becoming the main event as consumers seek whole-food sources of protein and fibre that are also budget-friendly and gut-friendly.
From brothy butter beans and crispy chickpeas to lentil-forward bowls and heirloom bean stews, chefs are increasingly treating legumes as premium ingredients rather than pantry basics. Social media is helping fuel the shift too, with viral dense bean salads, cosy “beans on toast” reinventions and aesthetically styled pantry content (dubbed BeanTok) centred around colourful heirloom varieties.
Try the Trend: Odysea Gigantes Beans In Tomato Sauce, Bold Bean Co Queen Butter Beans, Baked Masala Beans and Baked Smoky Chilli Beans, Brindisa Alubia Haricot Beans.
Beautrition
Glowing skin is becoming an inside job, as food, beauty and wellness continue to overlap.
Consumers are turning to ingredients rich in collagen, antioxidants, healthy fats and hydration, while products including collagen jelly sticks, olive oil shots and sea moss are blurring the lines between snack, supplement and skincare.
Nutrient-dense foods including sardines and oysters are gaining attention in the beauty conversation, alongside ingredients such as carrots, cucumber and cabbage.
Try the Trend: Doughlicious Collagen Banana Chocolate Chip Skillet Cookie, Whole Foods Market Freekeh, Chickpea and Pomegranate bowl, Sea Sisters Cornish Sardines with Rosemary and Capers, Freja Chicken, Ginger & Turmeric Sipping Bone Broth, Free Soul CreaGlow, Freja Chocolate Collagen Protein Shake, Linwood’s Psyllium Husk.
The Yōshoku Effect
Japanese comfort food is set to make a bigger mark in the UK in 2027, with growing interest in yōshoku – Japanese interpretations of Western dishes.
Think tonkatsu, Japanese curry rice, omelet rice (omurice) and Wagyu hamburger steak (hambagu), alongside konbini-inspired katsu and tamago sandwiches.
Social media is accelerating discovery through viral omurice, shio pan and Japanese convenience-store content, while the trend is increasingly moving from restaurant menus into grocery aisles through sauces, bakery products, snacks and ready meals.
Try the Trend: Dream Sake Daiginjo Sake, Jude’s Matcha Ice Cream, Little Moon’s Green Tea Mochi, Ombars Oat Milk Matcha Latte Filled Bar, Clearspring Matcha Misa Maple Biscuits, XOXO Prebiotic Grape Kyoho Soda, Nudie Snacks Katsu Curry Cauliflower Crisps.
Bitter Done Better
Customers aren’t simply tolerating bitterness – they are actively seeking it out.
As palates become more adventurous, bitter ingredients are showing up on restaurant menus and in packaged goods and beverages – from amaro-inspired non-alcoholic serves to chocolate enhanced with ingredients like fennel pollen, tarragon, burnt sugar, liquorice root, ash and quinoa. Grocers are also offering more bitter greens, like radicchio, endive, escarole, broccoli rabe and dandelion greens. Meanwhile, social media continues to fuel curiosity around licorice, salmiak, bitter melon and other intensely bitter or herbal flavour experiences.
The trend is being driven by a combination of expanding tastes, digestive wellness and the growth of the sober-curious movement.
Try the Trend: Botivo Batch 46 Non-Acholic Aperitivo, The Dessert House Black Forest Tiramisu, Soul Fruit Chewy Mandarin Slices, Ocelot Chocolates Organic Dark Chocolate + Lemon Olive Oil, FATSO dark chocolate bars range.
Terroir’s New Territory
The idea of Terroir – the soil, climate and geography that shape a product’s taste and character – is moving far beyond the wine aisle.
Interest in provenance and Protected Designations of Origin are drawing customers to the distinct flavours of regional honey, single-estate chocolate, named-source grains and products with a stronger connection to where they were grown or made.
The concept has even expanded into categories like seafood through “merroir,” which highlights how the ocean environment influences flavour.
Try the Trend: Whole Foods Market Parmigiano Reggiano, Whole Foods Market Carlingford Oysters, Principe San Daniel Prosciutto, Lykke Coffee Ugandan Single Origin, Cox & Co Chocolate Aleppo Chilli & Cherry, Sea Sisters Cornish Sardines with Chilli Oil.
Dish Reinvention
Some of 2027’s most exciting foods may not necessarily taste new – they will simply appear in unexpected forms.
Consumers are increasingly embracing playful mash-ups and reinventions of beloved dishes into entirely new forms, from birria ramen and smash burgers tacos to cinnamon rolls focaccia.
Restaurants and food brands are also fuelling the trend with inventive creations like Korean BBQ-inspired duck confit and mango sticky rice ice cream.
Try the Trend: Whole Foods Market Iced Berry Chantilly Matcha Latte, Whole Foods Market Chicken and Stuffing Pie, Esti Everything But The Bagel Dip, Fleur De Lan Croissant Crisps, YEW Pickle Sparkling Water.
Ingredient Minimalism
When it comes to ingredient lists, less is becoming more.
Growing scrutiny around additives and ultra-processed foods (UPF), alongside viral “read your labels” content, is encouraging some consumers to seek out products with simpler formulations and recognisable ingredients.
Manufacturers are responding by simplifying ingredients lists, while new apps are emerging to help shoppers navigate products on shelf. Whole Foods Market’s own Quality Standards currently ban more than 300 food ingredients.
Try the Trend: Whole Foods Market Paleo Salmon and Chicken, Dorset Dairy Yoghurts, The Coconut Collab 100% Coconut Water, Cru8 Kaley Cheesy Keto Crisps, True Dates Sour Cola.
Zero Waste 2.0
The next phase of zero waste is moving beyond simply throwing less away.
Food and drink brands are increasingly looking at ways to build more circular systems, using ingredients and by-products that may previously have gone unused.
Rubies in the Rubble transforms surplus fruit and vegetables into condiments, while DASH Water uses wonky fruit that might otherwise go to waste to flavour its sparkling drinks. Elsewhere, Nibs Etc. gives ingredients such as leftover fruit and vegetable pulp a second life, turning food by-products into granola and other everyday products.
Retailers are also continuing to explore refill models, bulk formats and partnerships designed to keep food out of landfill.
Try the Trend: Whole Foods Market bulk bins and Make Your Own peanut butter machines, Rubies in the Rubble Vegan Mayonnaise and Mustard, Dash Water range, Nibs Etc. Honey Oat and Almond Granola, Face Off Oil Milk Cleanser, Northern Pasta Co. Range.

items.title: Duvo raises $32 million Series A to become the one platform enterprises run their operations on

The round brings Duvo’s total funding to $48 million and will fund its expansion, starting with retailers and CPG companies. Two executives lead the expansion. Michael Green joins from Databricks as chief […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Duvo today announced a $32 million Series A led by Balderton Capital, with participation from existing investors Index Ventures, Northzone and Credo Ventures. The round brings Duvo’s total funding to $48 million and will fund its expansion, starting with retailers and CPG companies. Two executives lead the expansion. Michael Green joins from Databricks as chief commercial officer. He previously served as a senior vice president at Salesforce. Spencer Insolia recently joined as managing director, U.S. He was previously president of Kmart and a managing director at Accenture.
Duvo is the Enterprise Execution OS: one platform where a company’s operations run, with governed processes and clear user approvals. Duvo is built so that AI in operations doesn’t stop at the pilot. Every process a company adds runs on the same connections, the same approval rules and the same record of results, instead of becoming another standalone project.
The platform works the same way for every process. Duvo Clarity captures how the work really runs, through AI-led discovery interviews with the people who do it, screen recordings and existing documents. Duvo’s agents then run the approved steps across ERPs, supplier portals, spreadsheets and inboxes, through APIs where they exist and through the same screens people use where they don’t. That’s why Duvo can be live in weeks with the first process without a small army of engineers or a major systems integration project.
Decisions and exceptions go to the person who owns them, and operating cockpits show what is waiting for a decision and what the process delivered. Most companies run on systems that don’t talk to each other, and the manual work in those gaps is where value leaks. Duvo runs that work on one platform and recovers the value.
Gartner projects spending on business orchestration and automation technologies will exceed $21 billion by 2029, as enterprises consolidate fragmented automation tools onto a single platform. But turning that into operational results is proving hard. Gartner predicts that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 because of escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. In a separate survey of 350 executives at companies with $1 billion or more in revenue, Gartner found that those reporting higher returns from AI agents and automation had cut staff about as often as those with modest or negative results.
“For a while I measured AI in heads, counting how many people an agent could replace. It’s the wrong unit,” said Tomáš Čupr, co-founder and CEO of Duvo and founder and Group CEO of Rohlik Group. “At Rohlik, the gains I’d point to came from work nobody had the hours for. Our planners used to check about eight at-risk products a day per market for shortages. Now every signal gets checked, around the clock. We think of it as raising the GDP of every employee: more value from the people a company has, not the same value from fewer of them.”
Duvo has unlocked over $100m+ for its clients, across finance, supply chain, commercial, customer care, marketing and HR. At Notino, Europe’s largest online beauty retailer, those results span finance, customer care and marketing. Its quarterly reconciliation of about $45 million a year in supplier bonuses went from 70 days to 15, and from around 120 specialist hours per cycle to under 10.
“Our business processes have evolved over decades, and Duvo gives us a way to understand them in detail, and quickly,” said Gordon MacPherson, group productivity director at UK supermarket chain Morrisons. “It means decisions about which repetitive everyday tasks to simplify, redesign and automate can be based on evidence rather than assumptions. That gives us a much clearer path from identifying AI opportunities to putting them into operation, freeing up our people to concentrate on high-value work for the benefit of colleagues and customers.”
“Getting AI agents to work reliably across the enterprise remains incredibly difficult,” said Rob Moffat, partner at Balderton Capital. “Duvo’s unique ability is in how it uses AI to capture how work actually happens in the enterprise and what the causes of loss are. Duvo then automates these processes in the same integrated system. This is only possible with the deep operational experience of the founder Tomáš who previously founded three companies including Rohlik, the leading online grocer. Feedback from customers and consultancy partners is off the charts positive. We are looking forward to supporting Tomáš and team as they build the global leader in this segment.”
Duvo is model-agnostic, so the AI underneath can change without rebuilding the processes on top of it. Companies with stricter security or sovereignty requirements can run open-weight models on dedicated GPUs, connect a model in their own cloud or on-premises, or use an AI endpoint they already approve. Every approval and every change written back to a company’s systems is recorded. Duvo is SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 certified, and U.S. companies can buy it through Microsoft’s Azure Marketplace.
“Our clients don’t need more AI pilots. They need operations that actually change,” said Jan Hejtmánek, partner and AI institute leader at Deloitte Central Europe. “Through our alliance with Duvo, we combine Deloitte’s transformation expertise with an Enterprise Execution OS that maps how processes really work and then runs them, with people in control.”
“I’ve spent half my career as a retail operator and half as a consultant, and the same gap showed up from both sides: the insight was there, the execution rarely followed. Duvo closes that gap, and that’s why I’m here,” said Spencer Insolia, managing director, U.S. at Duvo.
“We’re starting in the U.S. with retailers and consumer goods companies, because that’s the work we know best,” said Čupr. “But the processes we start with, like freight and invoice audit, aren’t unique to retail.”
Christoph Schwaiger, former CEO of Aldi South Holdings, has also joined as Senior Advisor for Europe.
U.S. companies can start with one process, such as freight audit or payables audit, or with a free process map.

items.body:
Independent retailers across the UK have raised more than £10 billion for Good Causes by selling National Lottery tickets, new data from Allwyn UK, operator of The National Lottery, has revealed.
The milestone figure has been raised by corner shops across the UK since The National Lottery launched in 1994. On average, 23p of every pound spent on The National Lottery goes to Good Causes, which has supported more than 680,000 projects across arts, community, heritage and sports since its launch in 1994.
Today, over 22,000 independent retailers sell National Lottery tickets and scratchcards, and of those, 1,623 shops have raised more than £500,000, 469 have raised more than £1m, and 28 have broken the £2m mark. Remarkably, two shops have each raised more than £3m for Good Causes.
Three such retailers, located in Kent, Wales and West Yorkshire, have been recognised as part of Allwyn’s ‘Local Retail Champions’ initiative, each receiving a visit from a famous face that has benefited from National Lottery funding. A further six stores, located in Bristol, Manchester, Belfast, Glasgow, Ilkeston and Gateshead will feature in a secondary phase of the campaign.
Alastair Ruxton, Chief Impact Officer, Allwyn UK, said: “Most people in the UK live within half a mile of a Lottery funded Good Cause project, in no small part due to the extraordinary efforts of independent retailers who sell National Lottery tickets.
“The remarkable £10 billion local retailers have raised for Good Causes around the country has helped train Olympic and Paralympic athletes, fund award-winning British films and our world-renowned brilliant museums and galleries, as well as supporting thousands of vital community, education and heritage projects.”
Community Champions
Monty Dipoti, owner of Todmorden News in West Yorkshire, has raised more than £2.3m for Good Causes since taking over the shop 16 years ago. He was visited by Yorkshire local Nicola Adams, the first female boxer to become an Olympic champion after winning gold at London 2012 who was supported throughout her career with National Lottery funding.
Monty and Nicola visited Northern Powerhouse Boxing Academy, the UK’s first women-led boxing club, which received £250,000 of Lottery funding following a flood.
Kuljit Singh, owner of Premier Grand Avenue Stores in Cardiff, has raised more than £1m for Good Causes during his time running the shop. He was treated to a surprise visit by Joanna Page, star of Gavin and Stacey and Welsh icon. Together they visited Ministry of Life Education (MOLE), a National Lottery-funded education and outreach provider based in Cardiff that supports young people who are disengaged from mainstream education or at risk of leaving school without qualifications.
Steve Weight has run Borough Green Stores in Kent for 32 years, raising more than £1.4m for Good Causes in that time. He was surprised by local hero Matt Weston, double Olympic gold medal skeleton racer at the 2026 Winter Olympic Games, who grew up just down the road in Sevenoaks and benefited from funding through UK Sport’s Elite Athletes programme.
Matt and Steve visited Charlie’s Angels Kitchens, a local not-for-profit organisation focused on tackling both food poverty and food waste, that has received £20k of Lottery funding thanks to retailers like Steve.
Nicola Adams said: “I would not have won Olympic gold were it not for the funding made possible by incredible independent retailers like Monty – they are the heartbeat of their local communities. Thanks to their hard work, Good Causes like The Northern Powerhouse Boxing Academy get the support they need, guiding the way for the next generation of Olympians.”
Joanna Page said: “The funds raised by corner shops around the country are vital for the UK’s arts and creative industries. I grew up going into shops just like Kuljit’s, they are the backbone of our high streets. Seeing the incredible work done by MOLE, funded by the hard work of people like Kuljit, is an inspiration.”
Matt Weston said: “I should really give one of my gold medals to Steve. I cannot overstate the importance of the funding I’ve received from The National Lottery, and shop owners like Steve deserve a huge amount of credit for their role in raising it. He really is a local hero.”
The campaign is supported by Allwyn’s Social Value Fund, which the company has committed to invest in social value initiatives.

"Our business processes have evolved over decades, and Duvo gives us a way to understand them in detail, and quickly," says Gordon MacPherson, Group Productivity Director at Morrisons. "It means decisions about which repetitive everyday tasks to simplify, redesign and automate can be based on evidence rather than assumptions. That gives us a much clearer path from identifying AI opportunities to putting them into operation, freeing up our people to concentrate on high value work for the benefit of colleagues and customers."
"Getting AI agents to work reliably across the enterprise remains incredibly difficult," comments Rob Moffat, Partner at Balderton Capital. "Duvo's unique ability is in how it uses AI to capture how work actually happens in the enterprise and what the causes of loss are. Duvo then automates these processes in the same integrated system. This is only possible with the deep operational experience of the founder Tomáš who previously founded three companies including Rohlik, the leading online grocer. Feedback from customers and consultancy partners is off the charts positive. We are looking forward to supporting Tomáš and team as they build the global leader in this segment."
"We're starting in the US with retailers and consumer goods companies, because that's the work we know best," says Čupr. "But the processes we start with, like freight and invoice audit, aren't unique to retail."
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
AI will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards, which celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world, have now closed for entries. Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Check out our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector.
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.

items.title: Wayfair among firms hit with £6m fine for ‘misleading’ sales tactics
items.summary: Online retail giant Wayfair is among three firms fined £6m by the competition watchdog for misleading sales tactics. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said on Wednesday it fined Wayfair £4.8m for misleading customers with false limited-time offers that did not end when they said they would. This follows an investigation in which the CMA [...]
items.body:
Wayfair among firms hit with £6m fine for ‘misleading’ sales tactics
Online retail giant Wayfair is among three firms fined £6m by the competition watchdog for misleading sales tactics.
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said on Wednesday it fined Wayfair £4.8m for misleading customers with false limited-time offers that did not end when they said they would.
This follows an investigation in which the CMA found products were advertised on Wayfair’s website through ‘Daily Deals’ and 24-hour ‘Flash Deals’, alongside messages such as ‘Here Today, Gone Tomorrow’ and countdown timers.
The competition watchdog’s probe found that many products remained available at the same price or lower after the stated deadline, meaning the time-limited offer was false.
“By stating these were one-day offers, people could have felt pressure to make a quick purchase so as not to lose out,” the CMA said.
Alongside Wayfair, the CMA fined home appliance retailer Appliances Direct £1.2m and ordered it to refund customers about £432,000, and City-based gym group Gold’s Gym, which was hit with a £45,000 fine and ordered to refund customers about £9,000.
The watchdog fined Appliance’s Direct for misleading time-limited offers, while it found Gold’s Gym failed to clearly list the total membership price, including the joining fee.
The chief executive of the appliance firm’s parent company, Buy It Direct Group, Nick Glynne, said in a post on LinkedIn the fine comes as “we fight the battle of our lives against an unprecedented wave of competition from Chinese traders, alongside rising employment costs, taxes and regulation.”
“Our controls were not adequate. But is this fine proportionate to the harm? In comparison, the average fine for corporate manslaughter is around £500,000,” Glynne said.
The competition watchdog said “all three parties engaged constructively with the CMA” and “admitted to breaking the law and agreeing to settle the case early with the CMA”, so they received a 40 per cent reduction in their fine.
“Whether buying a new sofa, a washing machine, or joining a gym, people should see genuine, accurate prices and offers – and decide for themselves whether they want optional extras. At a time when many households are carefully managing their budgets, people shouldn’t lose out because of misleading sales tactics,” Hayley Fletcher, senior director for consumer protection at the CMA, said.
“The time is up for this kind of behaviour. Businesses must treat their customers fairly and make sure they comply with the law, or risk hefty fines,” she added.
A Wayfair spokesperson said in a statement: “Although we believe the fine is excessive and disproportionate, we take the CMA’s findings seriously and we chose to settle so we can continue to focus on serving our customers.”
Gold’s Gym was contacted for comment.

items.title: Nearly half of AI shoppers say they abandoned a purchase over conflicting product details

The Adobe for Business survey of 1,011 US consumers who use AI assistants to research purchases found that 49% said they had […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Retailers are being urged to check what AI shopping assistants tell customers before Black Friday, after research found that nearly half of surveyed AI shoppers had abandoned a purchase over conflicting product information.
The Adobe for Business survey of 1,011 US consumers who use AI assistants to research purchases found that 49% said they had abandoned a purchase after information from an AI tool did not match the brand’s website.
The findings, published on October 5, also showed that 59% said inaccurate AI information reduced their trust in a brand, even when the brand had not produced the answer.
Thomas Phillips, co-founder and CEO of DTC SEO Agency, explains that being recommended by an AI assistant is only useful if the information helps customers make an informed purchase.
“An AI assistant could recommend your product and still give someone a reason to leave when they reach your website. If it tells them shipping is free and they discover a charge, they have to decide which information to believe.
That customer may have been ready to buy. Now they are checking the basics, and every unanswered question gives them another reason to look elsewhere.”
With retailers preparing their Black Friday promotions, Phillips recommends three checks to identify discrepancies that could undermine a sale.
1. Check the details that could change a buying decision
Start with a small selection of best-selling products and ask AI assistants the questions customers would ask before ordering. These could cover sizing, materials, compatibility, delivery costs or whether an item can be returned after opening.
Record the answer, the date and any sources provided, then compare the information with current product pages and policies. Repeat the checks to establish whether an error keeps appearing.
“A mention in an AI answer tells you very little on its own. Check whether it describes the right version of the product and gives the customer accurate information about what they are buying,” Phillips explains.
For a small retailer, start with the products that matter most to your sales. You do not need to inspect your entire catalog to find a problem worth fixing.”
2. Review old offers before launching new discounts
Old promotional pages, outdated shipping thresholds and inconsistent return policies can create confusion before a customer reaches the checkout.
Retailers should review previous offers alongside their planned Black Friday promotions, making it clear when each offer applies, which products qualify and what conditions customers need to meet.
“Imagine someone arriving expecting last year’s discount because an old offer page is still easy to find. Even if your current promotion is clear, they are starting with an expectation you cannot meet.
Put the relevant terms close to the offer. A customer should not have to open three separate pages to work out what they will pay.”
3. Find where incorrect information is coming from
When an AI answer contains an error, check any cited pages to understand what may be causing it.
The source could be an outdated retailer listing, contradictory information on the brand’s website or an unsupported claim generated by the assistant. Identifying the source helps retailers decide what they can correct.
“Correct information you control and request updates where another website has the details wrong. You cannot guarantee what an AI tool will say, but you can remove avoidable contradictions from the information customers use to check its answer,” Phillips adds.
Before Black Friday, ask what a shopper might believe about your product before they arrive. Then check whether your website gives them a clear, accurate answer at the point they are deciding to buy.”

items.body:
Co-op Franchise, part of Co-op Wholesale, has successfully opened three new University stores this term.
The convenience stores are all based at highly esteemed Universities and are already operating well, serving their communities with essential food to go, meal solutions, snacks and treats and essential non-food items all at excellent value to meet students’ demands.
Queen Mary University of London was the first to launch on 10 September, followed by the University of Leicester on 17 September and most recently, University of Glasgow, which started trading on 23 September.
All located on campus, the convenience outlets are perfectly positioned to serve students and lecturers alike as they go about their day. It also marks the debut Co-op franchise store at a campus-based London University – a key milestone for the growing business area.
Since opening its first University franchise store in 2019, Co-op has steadily expanded its presence across the sector, working alongside universities and students’ unions to develop convenience stores designed specifically around the needs of students, staff and visitors alike.
Universities and students’ unions choosing the Co-op franchise model gain access to one of the UK’s most trusted retail brands, alongside proven retail expertise, operational support, technology platforms and a nationally recognised supply chain. The model enables partners to benefit from a professionally managed retail offer without needing to develop specialist convenience retail expertise themselves.
The partnership model aligns particularly strongly with the values of the higher education sector through Co-op’s long-standing commitment to ethical business practices, sustainability and community impact.
Melanie Crunkhorn, business development manager – Franchise at Co-op Wholesale, said: “All three of the new University Franchise Co-op store openings have been welcomed with open arms. They’re already trading well – it’s great to see what a useful resource they have become to the specialist customer-base they serve. We’ve taken immense pride in working alongside them to set them up for success and look forward to supporting them closely going forward.”

items.body:
In a shake-up to the e-commerce shopping customer subscription market, AliExpress, the international online retail marketplace, has launched Elite, the membership programme, rewarding its most loyal shoppers with exclusive discounts, fast delivery and dedicated service.
Unlike other rival membership schemes, AliExpress Elite is free of charge and applies to customers who have spent more than approximately £600 and placed orders on at least five days in the past year.
Eligible members who qualify will see their membership directly in the AliExpress app, along with exclusive Elite pricing on a wide variety of products.
Elite member benefits include:
- Extra discount: members enjoy an additional 5% discount on millions of products marked with the distinctive “Elite” label. This includes items across the Brand+, Choice and Local+ range.
- Bigger savings on Elite Day: The first day of every month is Elite Day on AliExpress. Members enjoy a higher 8% discount on eligible products.
- Simplified free returns: Members can return eligible products within 15 days of delivery, with no additional evidence required, for a hassle-free returns experience.
Commenting on the launch, Eric Zhang, Vice President of AliExpress, said: “Elite is our way of thanking the shoppers who choose AliExpress time and again. We want membership to offer practical value that customers can use as they shop, so we’ve made it free to join and focused the benefits on savings and convenience. Members can get extra savings on millions of eligible products, access bigger discounts on Elite Day and enjoy simpler returns.
“As we head into 11.11, eligible members will have another opportunity to save: on eligible products, they can combine their Elite discount with sale prices. We’ll continue looking for ways to make shopping on AliExpress more rewarding for the people who keep coming back.”
Warm up to 11.11 Global Shopping Festival
The Elite launch is coming as AliExpress prepares for its annual 11.11 Global Shopping Festival, running from 1-18 November, the platform’s biggest shopping event. Elite members will be able to stack their membership discount on top of 11.11 sale prices across ranges including Brand+, giving them enhanced savings to help them make their money go even further this 11.11.
Commitment to customer value
The Elite membership marks a significant milestone in AliExpress’s evolution as a destination for customers seeking value, quality products, convenience and excellent service. By offering upgraded benefits and a distinctive premium experience through a free membership programme, AliExpress is investing in long-term customer loyalty, rewarding the shoppers who have been loyal to the shopping platform by delivering tangible value that goes beyond price alone.
Elite membership is available now to all eligible consumers via the AliExpress app.

items.title: schuh marks Black History Month with a curated Community Window takeover on Manchester’s Market Street

Butterfly Future is a Manchester-based not-for-profit and social enterprise committed to breaking down barriers and creating opportunities […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Fashion footwear retailer schuh is marking Black History Month this October with a curated Community Window takeover on Manchester’s Market Street, created in collaboration with Butterfly Future and artist Obiaje Andrew Ejiga celebrating Black creativity, community and connection. Butterfly Future is a Manchester-based not-for-profit and social enterprise committed to breaking down barriers and creating opportunities for people and communities that are too often underserved through music, sports and the arts.
The latest edition of schuh’s Community Window which launched the beginning of October, spotlights Manchester-based visual artist Obiaje Andrew Ejiga, a Nigerian-born artist whose mixed-media practice combines oil painting and textiles to explore identity and culture through themes of double consciousness, assimilation and intersectionality.
Obiaje showcased his artwork as a live installation in the schuh Market Street window on Monday 5th October where customers were encouraged to watch the artist at work and experience the artwork taking shape in real time.
HEADS Creative, a Manchester-based brand and production company co-founded by Liam Heeley and Molly Ball, has produced more than 140 events and activations since launching in 2022, creating opportunities for creatives across the city and providing spaces for connection and collaboration. The October takeover marks HEADS Creative’s fourth Community Window with schuh.
More than a visual display, this month’s Community Window will create a space for connection, creativity, wellbeing and practical support. Throughout Black History Month, Butterfly Future founder Tabi Gazele and business partner Dre will host drop-in sessions in-store every Monday from 12:30pm, running for approximately 1.5–2 hours. Visitors will be able to meet Tabi and Dre, ask questions and access advice and support around navigating the creative industries, as well as discover upcoming Butterfly Future events and opportunities.
The space will also feature an interactive affirmation card colouring station, creating a relaxed environment for visitors to spend time, connect and get involved. Alongside the artwork and drop-in sessions, schuh will celebrate local voices through music, with an in-store playlist curated by Butterfly Future featuring a mix of independent artists and creatives from its community, including founder Tabi Gazele, alongside well-known Black artists and musicians. The playlist will play in-store throughout the month, bringing local voices and Black music into the wider Black History Month celebration.
Butterfly Future Founder, Tabi Gazele, said: “This is such a fantastic opportunity and we’re so happy that schuh is shining a light on the work Butterfly Future does in our local community and that we get to remind people during Black History Month that their wellbeing truly matters. Amazing!”
Obiaje Andrew Ejiga, Artist said: “Getting spotlighted by schuh means a lot to me. It’s a reminder to me that my work is good enough. At this stage in my career as an emerging artist, it’s really crucial for me to have my work shown in public settings. Being spotlighted as a young person gives me the necessary exposure I need at this point in my career.”
The initiative forms part of schuh’s ongoing commitment to transforming its stores into spaces of discovery, inspiration and belonging for its young customers and local communities. Following the launch of its Community Window scheme in March 2026, the platform has provided a revolving showcase for emerging creatives and offered a behind-the-scenes look at the people, practices and ideas shaping Manchester’s creative scene.
As schuh continues to invest in Manchester’s grassroots creative community, the October Community Window provides a platform not only to celebrate Black creativity and culture during Black History Month, but to create meaningful opportunities for people to connect, access support and discover what is available within Manchester’s creative community.
Visit schuh Manchester Market Street (31 Market St, Manchester M1 1WR) throughout October 2026 to visit the installation in person and drop in sessions with Tabi & Dre every Monday. Follow @schuh to discover more.

items.body:
Scotmid Co-operative has announced its UK-wide charity partnerships for 2026/27, with its retail businesses supporting air ambulance services across the communities they serve.
In Scotland, Scotmid Co-op and Semichem will support Scotland’s Charity Air Ambulance (SCAA).
In the North of England, Lakes & Dales Co-op, alongside the region’s Semichem store, will partner with Great North Air Ambulance Service (GNAAS).
And in Northern Ireland, Semichem will raise funds for Air Ambulance Northern Ireland (Air Ambulance NI).
Throughout the year, colleagues, members and customers will get behind their respective charity partnerships through fundraising, awareness activity and local events, helping each air ambulance service continue to deliver critical care in the communities it serves.
In Scotland, SCAA operates two helicopter air ambulances from bases in Perth and Aberdeen, responding to time-critical emergencies across mainland Scotland and its islands. As Scotland’s only charity-funded air ambulance service, it relies on public support to bring urgent care to people from cities and towns to rural and island communities.
The partnership between Scotmid Co-op, Semichem and SCAA was officially marked at the charity’s Perth base, where Scotmid colleagues met staff and crew and saw first-hand the work that goes into taking urgent care to people across the country. Scotmid’s support will also be recognised on SCAA’s helicopters.
Across the North East, North Yorkshire, Cumbria and the Isle of Man, Lakes & Dales Co-op and the region’s Semichem store will support GNAAS. The charity provides lifesaving critical care by air and road, operating from bases in Eaglescliffe in the North East and Langwathby, near Penrith, in Cumbria.
In Northern Ireland, Semichem colleagues and customers will raise funds for Air Ambulance NI, which works in partnership with the Northern Ireland Ambulance Service to provide the Helicopter Emergency Medical Service (HEMS). The service brings specialist pre-hospital care directly to people who are seriously ill or injured and can reach anywhere in Northern Ireland in approximately 25 minutes.
Karen Scott, Chief Executive Officer at Scotmid, said:
“We are incredibly proud that Scotmid Co-op, Lakes & Dales Co-op and Semichem will be supporting three vital air ambulance charities across the communities they serve.
“As a co-operative, supporting local people is at the heart of who we are, and this approach means our colleagues, members and customers can get behind the air ambulance service making a difference in their own communities.
“Scotland’s Charity Air Ambulance, Great North Air Ambulance Service and Air Ambulance NI all provide critical care to people facing the most serious illness or injury, often when every second counts.
“Our colleagues, members and customers have a fantastic track record of getting behind our charity partners. Together, we hope to raise vital funds, increase awareness of these lifesaving services and help their teams be there for people in their moment of greatest need.”
David Craig, Chief Executive of Scotland’s Charity Air Ambulance, said:
“Scotmid and SCAA share a very natural connection. We are both rooted in Scotland and focused on supporting people when and where they need it most.
“The support of Scotmid and Semichem colleagues, members and customers will help us reach emergencies across the country, from busy towns and cities to some of Scotland’s most remote areas.
“Every donation, fundraising event and conversation helps us reach more people and increase understanding of a service that can make a critical difference when every second counts.
“We are delighted to welcome Scotmid to the SCAA family and look forward to seeing what we can achieve together over the year ahead.”
Sophie Snowdon, Fundraising Manager at the Great North Air Ambulance Service, said:
“Lakes & Dales Co-op and Great North Air Ambulance Service share a strong connection through the communities we serve across the North.
“This partnership will help us continue to bring specialist pre-hospital care to people facing the most serious illness or injury, from busy town centres to rural and remote communities.
“Every donation, fundraising event and conversation will help support our teams and raise awareness of the difference they can make when every second counts.
“We are delighted to welcome Lakes & Dales Co-op and the wider Scotmid family as partners and look forward to seeing what we can achieve together over the year ahead.”
Kerry Anderson, Head of Fundraising at Air Ambulance NI, said:
“Semichem and Air Ambulance NI share a strong connection through the communities we serve.
“The support of Semichem colleagues and customers will help us bring specialist care directly to people facing the most serious illness or injury, wherever they are.
“Every donation, fundraising event and conversation helps keep our service flying and raises awareness of the difference HEMS can make when every second counts.
“We are delighted to welcome Semichem into the Air Ambulance NI family and look forward to seeing what we can achieve together in the year ahead.”
Fundraising will take place across Scotmid Co-op, Lakes & Dales Co-op and Semichem stores during 2026/27, with colleagues planning challenges, events and activities throughout the year and customers and members given opportunities to show their support.
Funds raised in each area will go to the charity serving that community: Scotland’s Charity Air Ambulance in Scotland, Great North Air Ambulance Service across the Lakes & Dales region, and Air Ambulance NI in Northern Ireland.

items.body:
One of the North West’s most loved retailers, Arighi Bianchi, has launched its first ever Christmas hamper collection, featuring festive food and drink including a selection of products from producers across the region.
The Macclesfield-based furniture and interiors retailer, which was established in 1854, has created six hampers for Christmas 2026, ranging from £85 to £160, with both alcoholic and alcohol-free options available.
The collection champions a number of North West names, with treats including Lancashire Tea, Wallings chocolates, Williams handmade Christmas cake and mince pie Eccles cakes, Fiddler’s Lancashire crisps, Stockley’s clotted cream fudge and Arighi Bianchi’s own ground coffee.
Celebrating its Italian heritage, there’s also some Italian favourites mixed in such as Vincenze Amaretti Biscuits, Natural Italian Olives, Crosta & Mollica Torinesi Breadsticks, Folonari Prosecco DOC Extra Dry and Baglio Gibellina Passiemento Nero d’Avola – Sicilian red wine.
Three sizes are available: the Boxed Hamper (£85), Medium Wicker Hamper (£130) and Large Wicker Hamper (£160), with an alcohol-free version of each at the same price.
Alcoholic hampers include Prosecco, while the largest hamper also features a bottle of Nero d’Avola red wine. Alcohol-free alternatives include drinks from Lancashire-based Mr Fitzpatrick’s, alongside Belvoir Elderflower Presse in the largest hamper.
The hampers can be sent directly to recipients with a personalised gift message, making them suitable for family and friends as well as corporate gifting. Businesses ordering five or more hampers receive £10 off each.
Orders should ideally be placed by 31 October, with deliveries beginning from 1 December 2026.

- Alcohol-Free Boxed Hamper – £85
- Medium Wicker Hamper – £130
- Alcohol-Free Medium Wicker Hamper – £130
- Large Wicker Hamper – £160
